title: Backend Developer
description: Step by step guide to becoming a modern backend developer in @currentYear@

questions.question: What is an inverted index and why is it faster than a SQL LIKE '%term%' query?
questions.answer: An inverted index maps each term to a posting list of the documents (and positions) containing it, so a search is a lookup of a few sorted posting lists plus an intersection, independent of total corpus size. A LIKE '%term%' cannot use a B-tree index because the pattern is unanchored, so PostgreSQL falls back to a sequential scan over every row. Lucene stores the term dictionary as an FST in memory and the postings on disk in compressed, skip-list-friendly blocks. The cost is that the index must be built at write time and only matches analysed tokens, not arbitrary substrings.

questions.question: Explain the analyzer chain in Elasticsearch and what breaks when index-time and search-time analyzers differ.
questions.answer: An analyzer is character filters → tokenizer → token filters; for example the standard tokenizer plus lowercase, stop and stemmer filters turns "Running Shoes!" into [run, shoe]. The same chain must produce compatible tokens at index and query time, otherwise a query token never matches an indexed token and you get zero hits with no error. A classic bug is indexing with an edge_ngram analyzer for autocomplete and also using it as the search analyzer, which explodes the query into every prefix and returns garbage — set search_analyzer to standard instead. Use GET /index/_analyze to see exactly which tokens each side produces before blaming relevance.
followUps: Why does a keyword field ignore the analyzer entirely?
How do you support multiple languages in one index?

questions.question: What is the text vs keyword distinction, and when do you use a multi-field?
questions.answer: A text field is analysed into tokens and is used for full-text relevance matching; it cannot be used for exact term matching, sorting or aggregation reliably. A keyword field is stored verbatim as a single token and is what you use for filters, term queries, sorting, and terms aggregations. When you need both — searching a product name and also faceting on it — you declare a multi-field: name as text with a name.keyword sub-field, which is the default dynamic mapping for strings. Getting this wrong shows up as a term query on a text field returning nothing because the indexed token was lowercased.

What is ignore_above on a keyword field for?

questions.question: A cluster becomes unstable after a service starts indexing arbitrary JSON from customers. What is mapping explosion and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: Dynamic mapping creates a new field for every new JSON key; if keys are user-controlled (for example event payloads keyed by id) the mapping grows to thousands of fields, and since the cluster state holding those mappings is replicated to every node, updates become slow and the master is overwhelmed. Guard it with index.mapping.total_fields.limit (default 1000), set dynamic: strict or dynamic: false on the offending object, and model variable data with the flattened field type or as an array of {key, value} pairs instead of arbitrary object keys. Fixing an exploded index requires reindexing into a correctly mapped one, because mappings cannot be removed in place.

questions.question: A document is indexed and a search one second later does not return it. Explain refresh_interval and near-real-time search.
questions.answer: Elasticsearch is near-real-time, not real-time: a document is written to the in-memory buffer and translog immediately, but it is not searchable until a refresh creates a new Lucene segment, which happens every 1s by default (index.refresh_interval) and only on indices that have been queried recently. So expect up to one refresh interval of lag. For read-your-own-writes use GET /index/_doc/<id>, which reads from the translog and is always current, or pass ?refresh=wait_for on the index request rather than ?refresh=true, which forces a segment and hurts throughput. For bulk loads set refresh_interval to -1 and restore it afterwards.

questions.question: How do you size shards for a log index that grows by 200 GB per day and is kept for 30 days?
questions.answer: Target 20–50 GB per shard and keep the total under roughly 20 shards per GB of JVM heap per node, because every shard is a Lucene index with fixed memory and file-handle overhead. 200 GB/day with one index per day and 5 primaries gives 40 GB shards, 30 days of retention is 150 primaries plus replicas — manageable. Use a data stream with ILM rollover on max_primary_shard_size rather than a fixed daily index, so a quiet day does not create tiny shards; then shrink/forcemerge to one segment when the index is read-only and move it to warm/cold tier. Over-sharding is the more common failure: thousands of small shards make the master slow and searches CPU-bound on coordination.

questions.question: How does BM25 score a document, and what levers do you have when relevance is wrong?
questions.answer: BM25 combines inverse document frequency (rare terms score higher), term frequency with saturation controlled by k1 (default 1.2, so the 10th occurrence adds little), and field-length normalisation controlled by b (default 0.75, so a match in a short title beats one in a long body). Levers: per-field boosts in a multi_match, function_score or a rank_feature field to fold in popularity/recency, a should clause on a phrase match to reward proximity, and tuning k1/b in the similarity settings. Use the _explain API on a specific document to see exactly which term contributed what before changing anything. Note that scores are computed per shard, so with few documents, dfs_query_then_fetch or a single shard avoids skewed IDF.

questions.question: You must change the mapping of a live 500 GB index with zero downtime. Describe the alias-based reindex procedure.
questions.answer: Applications should already read and write through an alias (products), never the concrete index name. Create products_v2 with the new mapping, run POST /_reindex with wait_for_completion=false and slices=auto to copy products_v1 into it, monitoring the task via _tasks. While reindexing, keep dual-writing new changes to both indices, or reindex with a range query on an updated_at field and then catch up the delta. Finally swap atomically in one call: POST /_aliases with remove products_v1 and add products_v2 as the same alias, verify, then delete the old index. The alias swap is atomic, so no request ever sees a missing index.
followUps: How do you handle deletes that happen during the reindex window?

questions.question: How do you keep Elasticsearch in sync with PostgreSQL as the system of record?
questions.answer: Do not dual-write from application code inside the request path — the two writes are not atomic and a crash between them leaves the index permanently wrong. Prefer change data capture: Debezium reads the Postgres WAL into Kafka and a consumer bulk-indexes into Elasticsearch, which gives ordered, at-least-once delivery that survives restarts. If CDC is too heavy, use the transactional outbox pattern (write the row and an outbox event in one transaction, a relay publishes it) — same guarantee, less infrastructure. Make the indexer idempotent by using the primary key as _id and external versioning (version_type=external with updated_at or the LSN) so out-of-order events cannot overwrite newer data, and schedule a periodic full reconciliation to catch drift.

questions.question: A search endpoint that paginates with from=10000&size=10 times out. Why, and what do you use instead?
questions.answer: Deep pagination requires every shard to build and sort from+size hits and send them to the coordinating node, so from=10000 makes each shard sort 10010 documents; index.max_result_window caps this at 10000 by default and beyond it the query is rejected or crushes heap. For user-facing infinite scroll use search_after with a tie-broken sort (for example [score, _id]), which is stateless and O(size) per page. For full exports use the point-in-time API plus search_after, or slice a scroll; classic scroll holds segment files open and is now discouraged for live traffic. If the UI truly needs jump-to-page-500, rethink the product requirement — no search engine does that cheaply.
followUps: Why does search_after need a unique tiebreaker field?

questions.question: What is the difference between the query context and the filter context, and how does it affect caching?
questions.answer: Clauses in query context (must, should) compute a _score, while clauses in filter context (filter, must_not, and everything inside a bool filter) answer only yes/no. Filters are cacheable: Elasticsearch keeps a bitset of matching documents per segment in the node query cache once a filter is used frequently on a segment of meaningful size, making repeated category/date filters nearly free. So put anything non-relevance — status, tenant id, date ranges, term filters — in filter, and leave only the actual text matching in must. A common performance bug is placing a high-cardinality term filter in must, which forces scoring work and defeats caching.
followUps: Why are now-based date ranges bad for filter caching?
How does a constant_score query fit in?

questions.question: Your cluster health goes yellow, then red, during a node restart. What do those states mean and what do you check first?
questions.answer: Yellow means all primary shards are assigned but some replicas are not — the cluster is fully queryable but has no redundancy; red means at least one primary is unassigned and part of your data is unreadable. Call GET /_cluster/allocation/explain to get the exact reason a shard is not allocating: disk watermark exceeded (low 85% / high 90% / flood_stage 95%, which sets indices read-only), a missing node holding the only copy, or an allocation filter/awareness rule with nowhere to place it. Yellow during a rolling restart is expected and resolves as the node returns; disable shard allocation with cluster.routing.allocation.enable=primaries before restarting to avoid needless rebalancing. Red that persists after the node returns usually means data loss on that shard and a restore from a snapshot repository.

questions.question: What are the architectural constraints of REST, and which one is most often skipped in practice?
questions.answer: REST defines six constraints: client-server, statelessness, cacheability, uniform interface, layered system, and optional code-on-demand. The uniform interface breaks down into resource identification via URIs, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages, and HATEOAS. The constraint almost always skipped is HATEOAS - most 'REST' APIs return plain JSON with no hypermedia links, which Roy Fielding's own critique says disqualifies them from being REST. Statelessness is also frequently violated by server-side sessions stored in memory.

questions.question: Explain the Richardson Maturity Model levels and place a typical CRUD JSON API on it.
questions.answer: Level 0 is a single endpoint tunneling everything over POST (RPC-over-HTTP, like SOAP). Level 1 introduces distinct resources (/orders/42) but still one verb. Level 2 uses HTTP verbs and status codes correctly: GET /orders/42 returns 200, POST /orders returns 201 with Location, DELETE returns 204. Level 3 adds hypermedia controls (HATEOAS) so responses carry links like {"rel":"cancel","href":"/orders/42/cancel"}. A typical CRUD JSON API sits at Level 2, which is where most teams deliberately stop because the tooling payoff of Level 3 is small.
followUps: What does Level 3 buy you that Level 2 does not?

questions.question: Which HTTP methods are safe, which are idempotent, and why is POST neither?
questions.answer: Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) must not change server state. Idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE) produce the same server state whether called once or N times - DELETE /orders/42 twice leaves the order deleted, even if the second call returns 404. POST is neither: it is defined as 'process this representation according to the resource's own semantics', so two identical POST /payments calls normally create two payments. That is exactly why POST needs an application-level idempotency mechanism.
followUps: Is PATCH idempotent?
Can a safe method still have side effects like logging or rate-limit counters?

questions.question: A mobile client on a flaky network times out during POST /payments and retries. The customer is charged twice. How do you design idempotency keys to fix this?
questions.answer: The client generates a UUID per logical payment attempt and sends it as the Idempotency-Key header; retries of the same attempt reuse the same key. The server stores (key, request fingerprint, response) in a table with a unique constraint on the key, inside the same transaction that creates the payment - so the insert either wins or violates the constraint. On a duplicate key with a matching request hash, replay the stored response including the original status code; on a mismatched hash return 422 (or 409) because the key was reused for a different body. Keys need a TTL (Stripe uses 24h) and in-flight requests must be handled with a lock or a 409 'request in progress' rather than a second charge.

Why store the request hash and not just the key?

questions.question: When do you choose POST vs PUT vs PATCH, and what are the semantics of each?
questions.answer: POST creates a subordinate resource where the server assigns the identifier - POST /articles returns 201 plus Location: /articles/9. PUT replaces the resource at a client-known URI in full; missing fields are treated as removed, and it is idempotent, so it can also create at that URI (upsert) returning 201 or 204. PATCH applies a partial modification, typically with application/merge-patch+json (RFC 7396, where null deletes a field) or application/json-patch+json (RFC 6902, an op array). PATCH is not inherently idempotent - a JSON Patch {"op":"add","path":"/tags/-"} appends each time it runs.
followUps: How do you make PATCH safe against lost updates?
Why is merge-patch unable to update a single array element?

questions.question: Distinguish 401 vs 403, 400 vs 422, and explain when 409 and 202 are the right answers.
questions.answer: 401 Unauthorized means authentication failed or is missing and MUST come with a WWW-Authenticate header - the client should re-authenticate; 403 Forbidden means the identity is known but lacks permission, so retrying with the same credentials is pointless. 400 Bad Request means the payload is malformed at the syntax level (broken JSON, wrong content type); 422 Unprocessable Content means the syntax is valid but the semantics fail validation, such as email format or a negative amount. 409 Conflict signals a state conflict - an optimistic-locking version mismatch, a duplicate unique field, or cancelling an already-shipped order. 202 Accepted means the request was queued for asynchronous processing; return a Location or a status URL so the client can poll the job.
followUps: Why do some APIs deliberately return 404 instead of 403?
What status do you return when a rate limit is hit, and which header accompanies it?

questions.question: A client reports that paging through /events?page=N&limit=50 skips and duplicates records during high write traffic. Diagnose and fix.
questions.answer: Offset pagination computes OFFSET N*50 against a live table; rows inserted or deleted before the current offset shift the window, so items get skipped or repeated between pages. It also degrades in cost because the database must scan and discard all skipped rows, so deep pages get slow. The fix is cursor (keyset) pagination: order by a stable, unique, immutable tuple such as (created_at, id) and query WHERE (created_at, id) < ($ts, $id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50, returning an opaque base64 cursor as next_cursor. Trade-off: no random page jumps and no total count, so keep offset only for small admin tables where 'page 7' matters.
followUps: Why must the cursor tiebreaker column be unique?
How do you support sorting by a mutable column with cursors?

questions.question: Compare API versioning strategies and say what actually counts as a breaking change.
questions.answer: Options are URI versioning (/v1/orders - most visible, cache- and log-friendly, but duplicates routes), custom header or media-type versioning (Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json - clean URIs, harder to test in a browser and often broken by caches), and query parameter (?version=2). Breaking changes are: removing or renaming a field or endpoint, tightening validation, changing a type or a status code, changing default values, or making an optional request field required. Adding optional response fields and new endpoints is additive, so clients must be built tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields. In practice most teams use URI versioning for major versions plus a deprecation policy with Deprecation and Sunset headers and a dated end-of-life.
followUps: How do you version only a single endpoint without bumping the whole API?
How would you measure which clients still use v1 before shutting it off?

questions.question: Explain ETag and conditional requests, and how you use them to prevent lost updates.
questions.answer: The server returns ETag: "abc123" (a strong validator derived from the representation or a row version) with a GET. On the next read the client sends If-None-Match: "abc123" and gets 304 Not Modified with an empty body, saving bandwidth. For writes the client sends If-Match: "abc123" on PUT/PATCH; if the resource changed meanwhile the server returns 412 Precondition Failed instead of silently overwriting another user's edit - this is optimistic concurrency control over HTTP. If-Match: * plus a create can also enforce 'only update if it exists', and Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since is the weaker second-resolution alternative.
followUps: What is the difference between a strong and a weak ETag?

questions.question: What is HATEOAS, and what real problem does it solve versus the cost it adds?
questions.answer: HATEOAS means responses embed the available state transitions as links, so a client discovers what it can do next instead of hardcoding URL templates - an order in state 'pending' includes a 'cancel' link that disappears once it ships. The benefit is that server-side workflow rules and URL structure can change without a client release, and the client's UI can enable actions directly from the links. The cost is bigger payloads, a media type that clients must understand (HAL, JSON:API, Siren), and client code that is significantly harder to write than fetch('/orders/42'). It pays off for long-lived public or machine-driven APIs and rarely pays off for a single-team backend serving one SPA.

questions.question: Your error responses are inconsistent across services. How does RFC 7807/9457 problem details standardize them?
questions.answer: RFC 9457 (which obsoletes RFC 7807) defines the media type application/problem+json with the members type (a URI identifying the problem class), title (a short human-readable summary), status (the HTTP code), detail (an explanation of this occurrence), and instance (a URI for this specific occurrence). Extensions are allowed as additional members, for example an errors array of field-level validation failures or a traceId. Clients switch on type, not on parsing prose from title, so wording can change without breaking anyone. Key discipline: the type URI should be stable and documented, and detail must never leak stack traces, SQL, or internal hostnames.

questions.question: What is the OpenAPI Specification, and what does a spec-first workflow look like?
questions.answer: OpenAPI (3.0/3.1; 3.1 is a full JSON Schema 2020-12 superset) is a machine-readable YAML/JSON description of paths, operations, parameters, request/response schemas, security schemes, and examples. Spec-first means the contract is written and reviewed before code: the spec lives in the repo, generates server stubs and typed clients (openapi-generator, oapi-codegen, orval), backs a mock server (Prism) so frontend work starts on day one, and renders documentation. CI then lints the spec (Spectral) and runs a breaking-change diff (oasdiff) against the main branch so removing a field fails the build. Code-first annotations are an acceptable alternative, but only if the generated spec is still diffed and linted in CI.

questions.question: A frontend deploy broke because the backend silently renamed a response field. Both sides had green unit tests. What testing would have caught it?
questions.answer: Unit tests with hand-written mocks cannot catch it because the mock encodes the old shape. Two complementary controls catch it: schema/contract validation of real responses against the OpenAPI spec in the backend's integration tests (Dredd, schemathesis, or a response-validating middleware in CI), and consumer-driven contract testing with Pact, where the frontend publishes expectations to a broker and the backend build fails verification if it stops satisfying them. On top of that, an oasdiff breaking-change gate on the spec in the pull request would have flagged the rename before merge, and can-i-deploy checks would block the release. The rule is: the spec must be generated from or verified against running code, otherwise it drifts.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a JWT, and what exactly does the signature guarantee?
questions.answer: A JWS-format JWT is base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature), where the header carries alg and usually kid, and the payload carries claims such as iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti. The signature guarantees integrity and authenticity - that the holder of the key produced these bytes and nobody altered them - but it does NOT provide confidentiality: the payload is base64url encoded, not encrypted, so anyone with the token can read it. That means no passwords, PII, or secrets in claims unless you use JWE. Verification must check the signature, exp/nbf, and iss/aud; skipping aud lets a token minted for another service be replayed against yours.

questions.question: HS256 vs RS256 for signing JWTs: when do you pick each?
questions.answer: HS256 is HMAC-SHA256 with one shared secret used for both signing and verification, so every service that validates tokens can also forge them - fine for a single monolith issuing and consuming its own tokens. RS256 (and ES256) is asymmetric: the issuer signs with a private key and consumers verify with the public key, published as a JWKS at /.well-known/jwks.json with kid-based key selection. Pick RS256/ES256 whenever tokens cross a trust boundary - multiple services, third parties, mobile clients, or any OIDC setup - because it enables rotation and revokes nothing from the verifiers' side. ES256 gives much shorter signatures than RS256 at equivalent strength, which matters for header size.
followUps: How does kid-based key rotation work without downtime?

questions.question: Explain the 'alg: none' and the HS256/RS256 algorithm-confusion attacks, and how to prevent both.
questions.answer: In the 'alg': 'none' attack the attacker strips the signature and sets the header algorithm to none; a library that trusts the header accepts an unsigned, attacker-authored payload. In algorithm confusion, a server that verifies RS256 is sent a token with alg switched to HS256, signed with the server's own PUBLIC RSA key as the HMAC secret - since the public key is published in the JWKS, the attacker can compute a valid MAC and the library verifies it if it picks the algorithm from the token. The fix in both cases is the same: never let the token choose the algorithm. Pin the expected algorithm at verification (jwt.verify(token, key, {algorithms: ['RS256']})), disallow none, and use typed key objects so an RSA public key cannot be used as an HMAC secret.
followUps: Why does an unpinned kid also enable key-injection via jku/x5u headers?

questions.question: Design refresh token rotation with reuse detection for a mobile app.
questions.answer: Issue a short-lived access token (5-15 minutes) and a long-lived, opaque, single-use refresh token stored hashed server-side with a family id. Every refresh call invalidates the presented token and issues a new access/refresh pair in the same family - that is rotation. If a refresh token that was already used is presented again, treat it as theft: revoke the entire family so both the attacker and the legitimate client are logged out and forced to re-authenticate, and alert. Store the refresh token in platform secure storage (Keychain/Keystore) on mobile or an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie on web, and handle the race where a flaky network causes a legitimate double-refresh by allowing a short grace window on the immediately-previous token.
followUps: How do you keep concurrent tabs from triggering reuse detection?
What do you log for a forensic trail when a family is revoked?

questions.question: An admin's account is compromised and you must log them out immediately, but your access tokens are stateless JWTs valid for one hour. What are your options?
questions.answer: A stateless JWT is valid until exp by definition - the only true fixes reintroduce state or shorten the window. Practical options: keep access tokens short (5-15 min) so revocation of the refresh token bounds the damage; maintain a denylist of jti values (or a per-user 'tokens_not_valid_before' timestamp) in Redis checked on each request, keyed only until exp so it stays small; or bump a per-user token version claim so all older tokens fail validation. The tokens_not_valid_before approach is usually best because it is one small key per affected user rather than a list per token. Emergency-only global invalidation can be done by rotating the signing key, at the cost of logging everyone out.
followUps: What latency and availability cost does the Redis check add to every request?
How do you propagate revocation across regions?

questions.question: How does HTTP Basic authentication work, and what must be true for it to be acceptable?
questions.answer: The client sends Authorization: Basic base64(username:password) on every request; the server returns 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="..." when it is missing. Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so the credential is effectively plaintext - it is only acceptable over TLS, and never with the credentials in a URL or a query string where they land in logs, proxies, and browser history. Because the password is replayed on every call, it must be verified against a slow hash (bcrypt/argon2), which makes it expensive per request unless you cache or issue a session/token after the first call. In practice it is fine for machine-to-machine internal calls and health endpoints, but for user-facing auth prefer a token flow since Basic has no logout, no scopes, and no expiry.

questions.question: Walk through the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE and name each party.
questions.answer: Parties: resource owner (the user), client (your app), authorization server, and resource server (the API). The client generates a random code_verifier, derives code_challenge = base64url(SHA256(verifier)), and redirects the browser to /authorize with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256. The user authenticates and consents, the authorization server redirects back to redirect_uri with a short-lived single-use code plus the state that the client must verify against CSRF. The client then POSTs to /token with the code and the original code_verifier; the server recomputes the challenge and, on a match, returns an access token (and optionally a refresh token and id_token), which the client sends to the resource server as Authorization: Bearer.

questions.question: What changes in OAuth 2.1 compared to OAuth 2.0, and why?
questions.answer: OAuth 2.1 consolidates the security best-current-practice into the core: PKCE is mandatory for all clients using the authorization code flow, not just public ones; the implicit grant (response_type=token) is removed because tokens in the URL fragment leak via history, referrers and logs; the resource owner password credentials grant is removed because it trains users to hand their password to third-party apps and blocks MFA; redirect URIs must be compared with exact string matching; and bearer tokens may no longer be passed in query strings. Refresh tokens for public clients must be sender-constrained or one-time-use with rotation. Net effect: authorization code + PKCE for user-facing apps, client credentials for machine-to-machine, device code for input-constrained devices.
followUps: What is a sender-constrained token (DPoP or mTLS) and how does it help?
