What is the risk of setting statement_timeout globally?

questions.question: What does the CAP theorem actually state, and why is "CA" not a real design choice?
questions.answer: CAP says that when a network partition (P) occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error response). Partitions are not a design option — packets get dropped, links fail — so P is always present in a distributed system. That leaves a real choice only between CP (refuse requests on the minority side, like a majority-quorum system such as etcd or ZooKeeper) and AP (keep serving possibly stale data, like Cassandra or Dynamo with low quorums). A single-node database is the only honest "CA" system, and it trades away partition tolerance by not being distributed at all.
followUps: Where does a Postgres primary with a synchronous standby sit on CAP?
What does 'consistency' in CAP mean compared with the C in ACID?

questions.question: What does PACELC add on top of CAP?
questions.answer: PACELC says: if there is a Partition (P), choose Availability or Consistency (A/C); Else (E), in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency (L/C). It captures the cost CAP ignores — even with a healthy network, strong consistency requires cross-node or cross-region round trips that add latency. DynamoDB default reads are PA/EL (eventually consistent, fast), while a strongly consistent read is PC/EC. Spanner is PC/EC: it pays TrueTime commit-wait latency to keep external consistency.
followUps: Classify Cassandra with QUORUM reads and writes under PACELC.
Why does cross-region synchronous replication make the EL/EC trade-off unavoidable?

questions.question: Compare range-based, hash-based, and directory-based sharding.
questions.answer: Range sharding assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (users A-F, G-M): range scans stay on one shard, but monotonically increasing keys (timestamps, auto-increment ids) send all writes to the last shard. Hash sharding routes by hash(key) % N or consistent hashing: distribution is even, but range queries fan out to every shard and adding a shard with plain modulo remaps almost every key. Directory sharding keeps an explicit lookup table mapping key to shard, giving full flexibility and easy per-tenant moves, at the cost of an extra lookup hop and a lookup service that becomes a single point of failure and must itself be cached and replicated.
followUps: How do you serve range queries on a hash-sharded table?
How would you shard a multi-tenant SaaS where one tenant is 40% of the data?

questions.question: One shard of eight is at 90% CPU while the rest sit at 15%. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.answer: This is a hotspot from a poor shard key. Diagnose by grouping recent queries by shard key value (top-N by request count and rows read) — typical causes are a low-cardinality key like country or status, a time-ordered key sending all new writes to the newest shard, or one whale tenant. Fixes: change the shard key to something high-cardinality (user_id, or tenant_id+entity_id composite), add a salt prefix such as hash(user_id)%16 + timestamp for time-series writes, or split the whale tenant onto dedicated shards via a directory mapping. Short term, add read replicas for that shard and cache its hottest reads while the reshard is prepared.
followUps: How do you change a shard key with zero downtime?
What metrics would have caught this before it became a page?

questions.question: You must grow from 4 shards to 6 without downtime. What is your plan, and how does consistent hashing help?
questions.answer: With hash(key) % 4 moving to % 6, roughly 2/3 of all keys change owner — an unacceptable full data reshuffle. Consistent hashing places shards on a hash ring with many virtual nodes each, so adding a shard only moves the keys in the arc it takes over, about 1/N of the data. The zero-downtime procedure: add the new shards to the ring, replicate the affected key ranges to their new owners in the background, run a dual-read (new shard, fall back to old) or dual-write phase while backfilling, verify with row counts and checksums, then flip the routing table and delete the stale copies. A common alternative is pre-splitting into many logical shards (e.g. 1024) mapped to few physical nodes, so growth is only remapping logical shards, not rehashing rows.
followUps: Why do consistent hashing implementations use virtual nodes?
How do you handle writes landing on the old shard during the migration window?

questions.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication, and when do you pick each?
questions.answer: In synchronous replication the primary does not acknowledge a commit until at least one replica has persisted the WAL record, so a primary loss costs zero committed data (RPO = 0) but every write pays the replica round trip and a stalled replica can block writes. In asynchronous replication the primary acknowledges immediately and ships WAL in the background, so writes stay fast but a failover can lose everything not yet shipped. Postgres offers a middle ground with synchronous_commit levels and synchronous_standby_names such as ANY 1 (s1, s2), giving durability against one node loss without waiting for all replicas. Use sync within a region for money-critical data, async across regions where the round trip would dominate latency.
followUps: What happens in Postgres if the only synchronous standby goes offline?
How do semi-synchronous replication in MySQL and ANY quorum in Postgres differ?

questions.question: Users report that right after saving a profile they see the old value, but a refresh a second later shows the new one. What is happening and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: Classic replication lag with read-your-writes violation: the write went to the primary, the following read was load-balanced to a replica that had not yet applied the WAL. Confirm with replica lag metrics (pg_stat_replication replay_lag, or Seconds_Behind_Master in MySQL). Fixes, cheapest first: route reads to the primary for a short window after a user's write (sticky session keyed by user id, typically a few seconds); or capture the write's LSN/GTID and have the replica wait for it before answering, so the read is causally consistent; or read from the primary only on endpoints that must be fresh. Reducing the lag itself (faster replica disks, fewer long-running queries blocking WAL replay, more parallel apply workers) is the durable fix.
followUps: How would you implement LSN-based read-your-writes at the connection-pool level?
Why can a long-running SELECT on a hot standby delay WAL replay?

questions.question: What is split brain in a replicated database, and how do you prevent it during failover?
questions.answer: Split brain occurs when a network partition leaves the old primary alive and reachable by some clients while a failover promotes a replica, so two nodes accept conflicting writes and the datasets diverge irreconcilably. Prevention rests on quorum: promotion requires a majority of an odd-sized cluster (or witness node), so a minority side can never elect a leader. Layer on fencing — STONITH, revoking the old primary's storage or VIP, or a lease with a monotonically increasing epoch/term that storage checks and rejects when stale. Tools like Patroni implement this with a DCS (etcd/Consul) leader key plus a TTL lease; the old primary demotes itself when it cannot renew the key.
followUps: Why is a 2-node cluster with automatic failover unsafe?
How does a fencing token prevent a paused old primary from writing after it resumes?

questions.question: What is a database index and how does a B-tree index make lookups faster?
questions.answer: An index is a separate, ordered data structure mapping column values to row locations, so the engine can find rows without scanning the whole table. A B+tree keeps keys sorted in a shallow, high-fanout tree (typically 3-4 levels even for hundreds of millions of rows), so a lookup is a handful of page reads — O(log n) — instead of O(n). Because leaves are sorted and linked, the same index also serves range scans (BETWEEN, >) and ORDER BY without a sort step. It does not help for predicates that are not sargable, such as WHERE lower(email) = ... unless you build a matching expression index.
followUps: When would the planner choose a sequential scan even though an index exists?
What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?

questions.question: Why does column order matter in a composite index? Given queries filtering on (tenant_id, status) and sometimes only status, what do you build?
questions.answer: A composite index is sorted by the leading column first, so it can be used only for a prefix of its columns: an index on (tenant_id, status) serves WHERE tenant_id = ? and WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ?, but not WHERE status = ? alone, because the status values are scattered across every tenant's subtree. General rule: equality columns first, highest selectivity first among equals, and the range or ORDER BY column last. So build (tenant_id, status) for the combined query, and add a separate index on (status, tenant_id) — or on status alone — only if the status-only query is frequent and status is selective enough to beat a scan.
followUps: What is an index-only scan and what does it require in Postgres?
When is a partial index (WHERE status = 'active') better than a full one?

questions.question: A team added nine indexes to a high-write table and insert throughput dropped by half. Explain the cost and how you would decide what to drop.
questions.answer: Every INSERT, DELETE, and any UPDATE touching an indexed column must maintain each index: more random page writes, more WAL/redo volume, page splits, and more buffer-pool pressure, so write cost grows roughly linearly with index count. Measure actual usage: in Postgres, pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan identifies indexes with zero or near-zero scans, and pg_index/pg_size_pretty shows what they cost in space. Drop unused indexes and redundant ones whose columns are already a leftmost prefix of another index — (a) is redundant when (a, b) exists. In Postgres, HOT updates only apply when no indexed column changes, so trimming indexes on frequently updated columns also reduces bloat and vacuum load.
followUps: How do you drop an index safely in production without blocking traffic?
Why can over-indexing make the planner pick worse plans?

questions.question: A read-heavy service is saturating its single Postgres primary. Walk through the scaling steps you would take, in order.
questions.answer: First exhaust the cheap wins: find the top queries with pg_stat_statements, fix missing indexes and N+1 patterns, and add connection pooling (PgBouncer) since idle connections alone can pin CPU. Next add caching for hot read paths, then vertical scaling if the instance is undersized. Then add read replicas and route read-only traffic to them, accepting replication lag and handling read-your-writes explicitly. Only when the write path or the working-set size exceeds one node do you shard, because sharding costs you cross-shard joins, distributed transactions, and global uniqueness; functional partitioning (moving a whole table family to its own database) is often the cheaper intermediate step.
followUps: What breaks in your application code the day you shard?
How do you enforce a globally unique username across shards?

questions.question: What is a shard key, and what makes a good one?
questions.answer: The shard key is the column (or set of columns) whose value decides which shard a row lives on. A good shard key has high cardinality, an even access distribution, and matches the dominant query pattern so most queries hit a single shard — for example tenant_id in a B2B product, or user_id in a consumer app. Bad keys are low-cardinality (country, status), monotonically increasing (created_at, auto-increment id), or misaligned with queries, which forces scatter-gather across all shards. Changing a shard key later means a full data migration, so it is one of the hardest decisions to reverse.
followUps: Why are cross-shard JOINs expensive?
How do you generate unique primary keys across shards without a central sequence?

questions.question: Compare cache-aside, read-through, write-through, and write-behind.
questions.answer: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and populates the cache itself — simple, resilient to cache outages, but the first request after every miss is slow and the app owns invalidation. Read-through pushes that miss handling into the cache library/provider, so the app only talks to the cache. Write-through writes to cache and database synchronously, keeping them consistent at the cost of higher write latency and caching data that may never be read. Write-behind (write-back) acknowledges the write into the cache and flushes to the database asynchronously, giving the fastest writes but risking data loss if the cache node dies before the flush.
followUps: Which pattern fits a write-heavy counter, and why?
Why is cache-aside the most common pattern in practice?

questions.question: On a write, is it better to update the cache or delete the key? Why?
questions.answer: Delete (invalidate) is usually safer. Updating the cache from the write path introduces a race: two concurrent writers can apply their cache updates in the opposite order from their database commits, leaving the cache permanently stale. Deleting means the next reader reloads the authoritative value from the database, and it also avoids computing derived values that may never be read. The standard order is write to the database first, then delete the key; for the residual race (a reader repopulating with a stale value read just before the commit) use delayed double-delete or bind the entry to a version/updated_at so a stale write cannot overwrite a newer one.
followUps: Why is 'delete cache, then write DB' worse than 'write DB, then delete cache'?
How does change-data-capture on the WAL improve invalidation reliability?

questions.question: How do you choose a TTL, and why is a TTL still needed when you invalidate explicitly?
questions.answer: Pick a TTL from how stale the data may be for the business and how expensive a recompute is: seconds for prices or inventory, minutes for feeds, hours for rarely changing reference data. Explicit invalidation is best-effort — a dropped event, a failed delete, a code path that writes without invalidating, or a bug will leave stale entries — so the TTL is the backstop that guarantees the error is bounded in time. It also caps memory for keys that stop being read. Add jitter (TTL plus a random percentage) so entries created together do not all expire in the same second and cause a synchronized miss storm.
followUps: What TTL would you give a user's permission set, and what else must you add?
How do you invalidate immediately across many application nodes?

questions.question: A popular key expires and the database instantly gets thousands of identical queries. What is this and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: That is a cache stampede (dog-piling / thundering herd): many concurrent readers miss the same key at once and all recompute it. Fix it by letting only one requester recompute: take a short-lived distributed lock (SET lock:key token NX PX 5000) and have the losers either wait briefly and retry or serve the stale value. Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) is often better — each reader recomputes with a probability that grows as the expiry approaches, so exactly one refresh typically happens before the entry dies and no request ever sees a miss. Complementary measures: store the value with a logical expiry longer than the physical TTL so stale-while-revalidate is possible, add TTL jitter, and pre-warm known-hot keys.
followUps: How do you release the recompute lock safely if the worker crashes?
How is a stampede different from a cache penetration attack?

questions.question: A single celebrity user's key is drawing so much traffic that one Redis shard is saturated while others idle. What do you do?
questions.answer: This is a hot key: sharding by key hash cannot help because all requests target the same key, so the shard hosting it is the bottleneck. Remedies: add a small in-process local cache (a few seconds TTL) in front of Redis so most requests never leave the app node; replicate the key under N suffixed copies (user:123#0..#9) and have clients pick one at random, accepting N-fold invalidation work; or use Redis read replicas for that shard. Also check the client is not doing a round trip per field — pipelining or a single hash fetch cuts request count. Detect these with redis-cli --hotkeys or the LFU-based OBJECT FREQ.
followUps: What consistency problem does replicating a key under 10 names create?
How would you detect a hot key before it saturates a node?

questions.question: Requests for non-existent IDs are hitting the database on every call because misses are never cached. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: This is cache penetration, and it is a cheap denial-of-service vector when the IDs are attacker-chosen. Use negative caching: store an explicit tombstone (empty value or null marker) with a short TTL, typically 30 seconds to a few minutes, so repeated lookups for a missing key are answered from cache. Keep the negative TTL much shorter than the positive one so a newly created entity becomes visible quickly, and delete the tombstone on create. For very large key spaces add a Bloom filter of existing ids in front of the cache: a negative answer is definitive and costs no cache or database lookup, while false positives just fall through to the normal path. Validate ID format first so obviously malformed keys never reach the cache at all.
followUps: What is the risk of a long negative TTL on a signup-name-availability check?
Why can a Bloom filter never give a false negative?

questions.question: Explain Redis eviction policies and which one you would set for a pure cache.
questions.answer: When memory hits maxmemory, Redis applies maxmemory-policy: noeviction (default — writes fail with OOM error), allkeys-lru / allkeys-lfu / allkeys-random (evict from all keys), and volatile-lru / volatile-lfu / volatile-ttl / volatile-random (evict only among keys that have a TTL). For a pure cache use allkeys-lru, or allkeys-lfu when the access pattern has a stable hot set and you want a one-off scan not to flush it, since LFU counts frequency rather than recency. volatile-* is right only when the same instance also holds keys that must never be evicted — and it will return OOM errors once no volatile keys remain. Never leave noeviction on a cache instance; that turns a memory-full condition into write failures.
followUps: Why is Redis LRU approximated rather than exact?
What happens to a cache instance running noeviction when it fills up?

questions.question: Explain the main Cache-Control directives for an HTTP response.
questions.answer: max-age=N sets how long a response is fresh in seconds; s-maxage=N overrides it for shared caches (CDN, proxy) only. public allows shared caches to store it, private restricts storage to the end user's browser (use it for anything per-user), and no-store forbids storing it at all. no-cache is not "do not cache" — it means store it but always revalidate with the origin before reuse. must-revalidate forbids serving stale content once expired, while immutable tells the browser never to revalidate within max-age, which is exactly right for content-hashed asset URLs such as app.9f3a2c.js with max-age=31536000.
followUps: Which header would you send on an authenticated JSON API response?
What is the difference between no-cache and no-store in practice?

questions.question: How do ETag, Last-Modified, and 304 Not Modified work together?
questions.answer: The origin sends a validator with the response: ETag (an opaque version token, usually a hash of the body) and/or Last-Modified (a timestamp with one-second granularity). When the cached copy goes stale, the client revalidates by sending If-None-Match: "<etag>" or If-Modified-Since: <date>. If the resource is unchanged, the server replies 304 Not Modified with headers and no body, so the client reuses its stored copy and only the headers cross the wire. ETag is more precise than Last-Modified because it detects sub-second changes and content that was rewritten with identical bytes; a weak ETag (W/"abc") signals semantic rather than byte-for-byte equivalence. The same If-None-Match / If-Match mechanism also powers optimistic concurrency on PUT, returning 412 Precondition Failed on a conflict.
followUps: Why can a gzip-rewriting proxy break ETags?
How would you use If-Match to prevent a lost update on PUT?

questions.question: What does stale-while-revalidate do, and how would you configure caching for an HTML page behind a CDN?
questions.answer: Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600 lets a cache serve the stale response immediately for up to 600 seconds past expiry while it refreshes the entry in the background, so users never wait on an origin round trip and the origin sees one refresh instead of a burst. Its sibling stale-if-error=86400 serves the stale copy when the origin returns 5xx or is unreachable, turning an outage into slightly old content. For an HTML page behind a CDN a common setup is Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600 plus an ETag, so browsers always revalidate but the CDN absorbs the traffic; add Vary: Accept-Encoding (and any header that changes the body) and use surrogate keys / tag-based purge to invalidate instantly on publish.
followUps: What goes wrong if you put a user-specific response in a CDN without Cache-Control: private?
Why is Vary: User-Agent almost always a mistake?

questions.question: After a deploy, some users still run the old JavaScript bundle for days. Diagnose and fix.
questions.answer: The asset was served with a long max-age under a stable filename (app.js), so browsers reuse the cached copy without revalidating until it expires — a CDN purge does nothing for copies already in browsers. Confirm by comparing the response headers and the ETag the browser sends on reload against the deployed file. Fix with content-hashed filenames (app.<contenthash>.js) served as Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, so a new deploy produces a new URL that is guaranteed to be fetched; the HTML entry point that references it must be short-lived (max-age=0, must-revalidate, or s-maxage with revalidation) so the new reference is picked up. To unstick users already holding the bad copy, change the URL and, if the app is long-lived in the tab, have the service worker or a version endpoint prompt a reload.
followUps: Why does a CDN purge not help here?
How does a service worker change the cache invalidation story?

questions.question: Why is MD5 acceptable for building a cache key but unacceptable for passwords or signatures?
questions.answer: A cache key only needs a fast, well-distributed fingerprint of the inputs — MD5 of a normalized query string gives a compact 128-bit key, and no adversary gains anything from a collision because a collision merely returns the wrong cached value, and even that is avoidable by including the raw inputs in the stored entry. MD5 is broken for security: practical collisions are computable in seconds (chosen-prefix collisions since 2009), so it offers no integrity guarantee for signatures or certificates, and it is far too fast — commodity GPUs compute tens of billions of MD5 hashes per second, so any password digest, salted or not, falls to brute force. Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id with a per-user salt for passwords, and HMAC-SHA256 or Ed25519 for signatures and message authentication. If the cache key is derived from attacker-controlled data and a wrong hit would leak another user's data, use SHA-256 instead — the speed difference is irrelevant at cache-key sizes.
followUps: Why is a fast hash specifically the wrong property for password storage?
When does a cache-key collision become a security bug rather than a correctness bug?

questions.question: A reviewer finds md5(file_bytes) used to deduplicate user uploads and md5(password + salt) in the login code. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: The password use is a critical bug: MD5 is a fast general-purpose hash, so an attacker with the database can try billions of candidates per second per GPU, and salting only stops precomputed rainbow tables, not brute force. Migrate to Argon2id (or bcrypt with cost >= 12), rehashing transparently on next successful login and wrapping existing digests in the meantime. The dedup use is mostly fine for accidental duplicates, but because MD5 chosen-prefix collisions are cheap, a user can deliberately upload two different files with the same digest and make one overwrite or shadow the other — so if dedup decides what content is served back, switch to SHA-256 and compare byte length too. Neither MD5 use should appear in anything a security decision depends on.
followUps: How do you migrate a password table off MD5 without forcing every user to reset?
What is a chosen-prefix collision and why does it matter for file dedup?

questions.question: What is the difference between a unit test, an integration test, and a functional (end-to-end) test?
questions.answer: A unit test exercises one module in isolation with its collaborators replaced by test doubles; it runs in milliseconds and fails for exactly one reason. An integration test wires real adapters together — service plus real Postgres, real HTTP client against a stub server — and proves the seams (SQL, serialization, transactions) actually work. A functional/E2E test drives the system through its public entry point (HTTP request in, HTTP response and DB state out) and asserts business outcomes, not internals. The trade-off is speed and fault localisation versus realism: unit tests tell you where it broke, E2E tests tell you that it is actually broken for users.
followUps: Where do you draw the boundary of a 'unit' — a class or a use case?
Why can a suite of 100% passing unit tests still ship a broken feature?

questions.question: Explain the test pyramid and the 'testing trophy'. When would you choose one shape over the other?
questions.answer: The pyramid (Cohn) says: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests, because cost and flakiness grow as you go up. The trophy (Dodds) puts the bulk of the investment in integration tests, with static analysis/types as the base and unit and E2E as thin layers, arguing that most real bugs live in the wiring, not in pure functions. Pick the pyramid when you have rich domain logic (pricing, scheduling, state machines) worth testing directly; pick the trophy when the service is mostly glue — HTTP handler, ORM query, external call — where a unit test with everything mocked only asserts that the mocks were configured. Modern containerized DBs made integration tests cheap enough that a trophy shape is viable where it once was not.
followUps: How does a hexagonal/DDD architecture change the ideal shape?
What is your target for total CI suite wall-clock time?

questions.question: Distinguish mock, stub, fake, and spy. Give a case where each is the right choice.
questions.answer: A stub returns canned data to drive a code path (a payment gateway stub returning DECLINED). A mock is a stub with assertions on the interaction — it verifies that charge() was called once with a given amount — so it tests behaviour, not state. A fake is a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository, in-memory bus) used when you need real semantics without real infrastructure. A spy wraps the real object and records calls, letting you assert an email was sent while the rest still executes. Use a fake for repositories, a stub for inbound data, a mock only for genuine outgoing commands you cannot observe otherwise, and a spy when you must keep real behaviour and still check a side effect.
followUps: Why is asserting on a mock of a query (not a command) usually a smell?
How do you keep an in-memory fake repository honest against the real SQL one?

questions.question: A team's unit tests all pass but every refactor breaks dozens of them, and production bugs still slip through. Diagnose the problem.
questions.answer: This is classic over-mocking: the tests assert interactions with mocked collaborators, so they encode the current call graph rather than observable behaviour. Renaming a method or moving a call between layers breaks tests even though behaviour is identical (false failures), while a wrong SQL query or a serialization mismatch passes because the real dependency was never executed (false confidence). The fix is to move assertions to inputs and outputs of a use case, replace mocked repositories with in-memory fakes or a real containerized DB, and reserve mocks for the few true external boundaries (payment provider, SMTP). Test the public contract of a module, not its private collaborators.
followUps: How would you migrate a large mock-heavy suite incrementally?
What metric would show the suite is improving?

questions.question: For integration tests against a database, would you use Testcontainers or an in-memory DB like H2/SQLite? Argue the trade-off.
questions.answer: Testcontainers runs the real engine (postgres:16 in Docker), so migrations, JSONB, arrays, partial indexes, CTEs, isolation levels, and vendor-specific SQL behave exactly as in production; the cost is Docker availability in CI and a few seconds of container startup, mitigated by reusing one container per suite and template databases or transaction rollback per test. An in-memory DB starts in milliseconds but is a different engine: H2's Postgres compatibility mode silently diverges on upserts, locking, and types, so tests can pass on a query that fails in production — the worst possible failure mode. Use Testcontainers as the default and in-memory only where the storage is genuinely trivial. Keep test isolation by wrapping each test in a transaction that is rolled back, or truncating tables between tests.
followUps: How do you keep a shared container from leaking state between parallel tests?
How do you test code that itself manages transactions?

questions.question: One CI job fails roughly 1 in 15 runs, always in a different test. How do you find and fix the flakiness?
questions.answer: First make it measurable: record per-test pass/fail history across runs so you can rank flaky tests instead of guessing, and quarantine the worst offenders out of the blocking path (never just add a blanket retry, which hides real races). Then reproduce: run the suite with a fixed but reported random seed, run it repeatedly (--count/-repeat), and run the suspect test alone versus in the full suite — if it only fails in the suite, the cause is shared state (leftover DB rows, a static singleton, a cache, a global clock). The usual root causes are order dependence, wall-clock and timezone assumptions, sleep-based waits instead of polling on a condition, unseeded randomness, unclosed connections, and parallel tests sharing a fixed port or fixed primary key. Fix by injecting a controllable clock, seeding randomness, isolating data per test (unique tenant/ids, transactional rollback), and replacing sleeps with explicit awaits.
followUps: When is auto-retry acceptable, and how do you stop it hiding real bugs?
How do you prevent quarantined tests from being forgotten forever?

questions.question: What is consumer-driven contract testing, and how does it apply to REST, gRPC, and GraphQL?
questions.answer: In contract testing, each consumer records the requests it makes and the response shape it needs; that pact is verified against the real provider in the provider's own CI, so the provider learns at build time that a change breaks someone — without running a full integrated environment. For REST, tools like Pact replay the interactions against the provider; for gRPC, the .proto is already a machine-checkable contract, so you add a buf breaking (or protolock) check plus pact-style verification of semantics; for GraphQL, the schema is the contract and you run a schema diff plus persisted consumer queries validated against the new schema, since a field removal only breaks the clients that actually select it. The key property is that contract tests are fast and run per-service, unlike E2E environments which are slow, shared, and flaky.
followUps: How do you handle a breaking change that every consumer must adopt?
Where does contract testing fail to catch a bug?

questions.question: A GraphQL query for 50 posts with their authors fires 51 database queries. What is happening and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: This is the N+1 problem: the posts resolver runs one query, then GraphQL invokes the author resolver once per post, each issuing its own SELECT. The standard fix is a DataLoader per request: resolvers call loader.load(authorId), the loader batches all ids collected within a tick into one SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ANY($1) and caches by key for the request lifetime only (a longer-lived cache would leak data across users and serve stale rows). Alternatives are a look-ahead resolver that inspects the selection set and issues a single JOIN, or projecting the query at the persistence layer. You also cap the blast radius with query depth limits, complexity scoring, and persisted queries so a client cannot request an arbitrarily deep graph.
followUps: Why must the DataLoader cache be scoped per request?
How would you detect N+1 automatically in CI?

questions.question: Which changes to a protobuf message are backward compatible, and which break existing gRPC clients? What are the four streaming modes?
questions.answer: Safe: adding a new field with a fresh tag number, adding a new RPC or service, adding an enum value (if clients tolerate unknown values), renaming a field (the wire format uses tag numbers, not names). Breaking: reusing or changing a tag number, changing a field's type in an incompatible way (int32 to string), moving a field in or out of a oneof, changing cardinality, and deleting a field without marking it reserved — a later reuse of that tag silently misinterprets old data. gRPC has four modes: unary, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming; streams are multiplexed over one HTTP/2 connection. Enforce compatibility mechanically with buf breaking against the main branch in CI rather than by review.
followUps: How do you test a bidirectional streaming RPC deterministically?
Why is a proto3 field with a default value indistinguishable from an unset one, and what do you do about it?

questions.question: You must integrate with a legacy SOAP service. What do WSDL and the SOAP envelope give you, and how do you test the integration?
questions.answer: SOAP is an XML messaging protocol: every message is an Envelope with an optional Header (WS-Security tokens, transaction context) and a Body; errors come back as a soap:Fault with faultcode/faultstring, typically over HTTP 500. The WSDL is the machine-readable contract — types (XSD), messages, portType operations, binding, and service endpoint — from which you generate a strongly typed client, so the schema is the contract and there is no need for hand-rolled parsing. For testing, generate the client from the WSDL, validate requests against the XSD, and run integration tests against a recorded/stubbed endpoint (WireMock or a SOAP mock server) since the real service is usually rate-limited and stateful. Wrap it in an anti-corruption layer so SOAP types never leak into your domain model.
followUps: How does SOAP differ from REST in error handling and transactions?
How do you handle WS-Security signing in tests?

questions.question: Compare cookie/session-based auth with token (JWT in header) auth. How do HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite change the risk profile?
questions.answer: Cookie sessions keep an opaque session id server-side, so revocation is instant and the payload leaks nothing; the browser attaches the cookie automatically, which is convenient but is exactly what makes CSRF possible. Set HttpOnly so JavaScript (and therefore an XSS payload) cannot read the cookie, Secure so it is only sent over HTTPS, and SameSite=Lax (default in modern browsers) or Strict so it is not attached to cross-site POSTs — SameSite=None requires Secure and reopens CSRF exposure. JWTs are stateless and scale across services but cannot be revoked before expiry without a denylist, and storing them in localStorage makes any XSS a full account takeover since the token is readable. In practice: short-lived access token plus refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie gives both statelessness and safe storage.
followUps: Why does SameSite not fully replace CSRF tokens?
How do you revoke a JWT that has 15 minutes left to live?

questions.question: A money-transfer endpoint can be triggered by a hidden form on an attacker's site while the user is logged in. Name the attack and the layered defence, and explain session fixation while you are at it.
questions.answer: That is CSRF: the browser attaches the session cookie to the cross-site request, so the server sees an authenticated user. Defences, layered: SameSite=Lax/Strict on the session cookie; a synchronizer token (per-session or per-request, validated server-side) or the double-submit cookie pattern; verifying Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site headers; and never using GET for state changes. Session fixation is a different attack: the attacker plants a known session id (via a URL parameter or a set cookie) before login, and if the server keeps that id after authentication, the attacker now shares the victim's authenticated session — the fix is to regenerate the session id on every privilege change (login, logout, role elevation) and to never accept session ids from the URL. Also set a short idle timeout and bind the session to a rotating fingerprint where it does not break legitimate users.
followUps: Why does a CSRF token not protect you if the site also has an XSS hole?
How do you protect a CORS-enabled JSON API from CSRF?

questions.question: OpenID Connect versus SAML: what are they, how do they differ, and when would you still pick SAML?
questions.answer: OIDC is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: the client runs an authorization-code flow with PKCE and gets back a JSON Web Token id_token (signed, claims like sub, iss, aud, exp, nonce) plus an access token, with metadata at /.well-known/openid-configuration and keys at the JWKS endpoint. SAML 2.0 is XML-based: the SP redirects to the IdP, which POSTs back a signed XML Assertion, usually via the HTTP-POST binding with an XML-DSig signature. OIDC is far better suited to mobile apps, SPAs, and APIs — JSON, small tokens, simple libraries — while SAML remains the requirement in large enterprises and government, where existing IdPs, ADFS, and procurement checklists demand it. If you support both, normalise at the edge into one internal session so the rest of the system never knows which protocol was used.
followUps: What does the nonce in an id_token protect against?
Why is XML signature wrapping a recurring SAML vulnerability class?

questions.question: How do you write automated tests for an SSO login flow without a real identity provider in CI?
questions.answer: Run a local IdP in the test environment — a container such as Keycloak or a mock OIDC provider — so the full authorization-code + PKCE round trip, the JWKS lookup, and signature validation are genuinely exercised; that catches issuer/audience misconfiguration that a mocked verifier would hide. For unit tests of the relying-party code, generate a keypair in the test, mint an id_token yourself, and serve it from a stub JWKS endpoint, then write negative tests: expired exp, wrong aud, wrong iss, tampered signature, replayed nonce, alg set to none — each must be rejected. For SAML the equivalent is a fixture assertion signed by a test certificate plus negative cases for expired NotOnOrAfter and signature-wrapping payloads. Never disable signature validation to make tests pass; that flag inevitably escapes into production config.
followUps: How do you keep test certificates from expiring and breaking CI?
What does a PKCE code_challenge protect against for a public client?

questions.question: What stages would you put in a CI/CD pipeline for a backend service, and in what order?
questions.answer: Fast feedback first: checkout, dependency restore from cache, lint and type check, unit tests — everything that can fail in under two minutes. Then build the artifact exactly once (container image or jar), run integration tests against that artifact with Testcontainers, run security gates (SAST, dependency/CVE scan, secret scan, image scan), and publish the artifact to a registry tagged with the immutable commit SHA. Deployment then promotes that same artifact through staging and production with smoke tests and a manual or policy gate before prod. The rule is build once, deploy many: rebuilding per environment means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.
followUps: Which stages would you run in parallel?
What belongs in a pre-merge pipeline versus a post-merge one?

questions.question: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment?
questions.answer: Continuous integration means every developer merges to trunk frequently (at least daily) and each merge triggers an automated build and test run, so integration problems surface in minutes instead of at the end of a sprint. Continuous delivery means every green build produces a deployable artifact that could go to production at any moment — the release itself is a business decision, triggered by a human. Continuous deployment removes that button: every commit passing the pipeline goes to production automatically. Moving from delivery to deployment requires trustworthy tests, feature flags for incomplete work, automated rollback, and good production monitoring.
followUps: What must be true before you can turn on continuous deployment?
How do trunk-based development and long-lived branches affect CI?

questions.question: Compare rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.
questions.answer: Rolling replaces instances in batches behind the load balancer: no extra infrastructure, but both versions serve traffic at once (so the code must be backward compatible) and rollback means another slow roll. Blue-green runs a full second environment, then flips the router in one step: instant cutover and instant rollback, at the cost of double capacity and the hard part of sharing one database between both colours. Canary sends a small slice (1%, then 5%, 25%...) to the new version while comparing error rate and latency against the baseline, automatically halting or rolling back on SLO breach — the best risk/cost balance, but it needs per-version metrics and traffic splitting at the proxy or service mesh. All three assume the new version is compatible with the data and with the old version still running.
followUps: How does a blue-green deploy handle a schema change?
What signals would you gate a canary promotion on?

questions.question: A release must rename a column and ship code that uses the new name. How do you order the deploy so it can be rolled back safely?
questions.answer: Never couple a destructive migration to the code deploy — use expand/contract across at least three releases. Expand: add the new column, backfill it in batches, and have the application dual-write to both old and new while still reading the old one. Migrate: deploy code that reads the new column (old column still written, so rolling back one version is safe). Contract: after the new version has been stable and no rollback target still needs it, stop writing the old column and drop it in a separate release. The invariant is that the schema must be compatible with both the current and previous application version at all times, because during a rolling or canary deploy both are live; also run migrations as a separate step before the app rollout, keep them additive and non-locking (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, no long ALTER on a hot table), and never write a migration whose rollback loses data.
followUps: How do you back out a deploy that already ran an irreversible migration?
How do you backfill 200 million rows without blocking writes?

questions.question: What problems do feature flags solve in a CD pipeline, and what problems do they create?
questions.answer: Flags decouple deploy from release: unfinished code can merge to trunk behind a disabled flag (keeping trunk-based development viable), a feature can be enabled for 1% of users or one tenant, and a bad feature can be turned off in seconds without a redeploy — a far faster rollback than shipping a new build. The costs are combinatorial explosion of untested code paths, flags that become permanent hidden configuration, and tests that only cover one side of the branch. Manage them as inventory: an owner and an expiry date per flag, a removal ticket created when the flag is created, flag state visible in logs and traces, and a distinction between short-lived release toggles (delete after rollout) and long-lived ops/kill switches (keep, and test both states).
followUps: How do you test a codebase with 30 interacting flags?
Should flag evaluation be cached, and what breaks if it is?

questions.question: Why must build artifacts be immutable, and how do you enforce that in practice?
questions.answer: If an artifact can change after it was tested, the evidence from CI no longer describes what runs in production — and an incident becomes unreproducible because you cannot get back the exact bits. Enforce it by tagging images with the immutable commit SHA (never deploying by :latest or a moving tag), enabling registry tag immutability, pinning by digest in the deployment manifest, and recording a provenance/SBOM attestation (SLSA, cosign signature) that ties the image digest to the source commit and build. Deployments then promote a digest between environments, with environment-specific values supplied as configuration, never as a rebuild. Reproducible builds and locked dependency files (package-lock.json, go.sum) close the remaining gap.
followUps: How do you handle a base-image CVE patch without breaking immutability?
What does deploying by :latest break during a rollback?

questions.question: Your pipeline takes 40 minutes and developers have stopped waiting for it. How do you cut it down?
questions.answer: Measure per-stage timings first, then attack the top items. Typical wins: cache dependencies and build outputs keyed by a lockfile hash (with a restore-key fallback so a near-miss still helps), order Dockerfile layers so dependency installation is cached and use multi-stage builds plus BuildKit cache mounts, run independent jobs in parallel, and shard the test suite across runners by recorded duration rather than alphabetically. Then reduce work: run affected-only tests for monorepo packages, move slow E2E suites out of the pre-merge gate into a post-merge or nightly run, and keep the pre-merge gate under about ten minutes. Verify the fix by tracking p50/p95 pipeline duration, and never cache anything keyed loosely enough to leak stale or cross-branch artifacts.
followUps: What should never be cached between runs?
How do you keep test sharding balanced as the suite grows?

questions.question: How do you handle secrets in CI/CD pipelines?
questions.answer: Secrets never live in the repository, in the Dockerfile, or in build args that end up in image layers — they come from a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub/GitLab secret store) injected as environment variables or mounted files at run time. Prefer short-lived, workload-identity credentials over static keys: OIDC federation lets a CI job assume a cloud role for minutes with no long-lived key to leak. Scope secrets per environment and per job, block them from pull-request builds of forks, enable log masking, and add a secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog) as a pipeline gate plus pre-commit hook. Rotate on a schedule and immediately on any exposure, and remember that masking is not protection against a malicious build step — review who can edit pipeline files.
followUps: Why is a secret passed via docker build --build-arg still recoverable?
How does OIDC federation remove the need for stored cloud keys?

questions.question: What does ACID mean, and what does each letter actually guarantee?
questions.answer: Atomicity: a transaction applies entirely or not at all — a partial commit is impossible, implemented with a write-ahead log and rollback. Consistency: the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting declared constraints (FK, unique, check) and the application's invariants. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not observe each other's intermediate state, to the degree the isolation level promises — READ COMMITTED still allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms, REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads, SERIALIZABLE gives the effect of some serial order (Postgres does this with SSI, aborting with error 40001 on a conflict). Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash, because the WAL was flushed to stable storage (fsync) before the acknowledgement.
followUps: Which anomalies does READ COMMITTED still permit?
How does synchronous_commit=off change the D in ACID?

questions.question: Should a whole HTTP request run inside one database transaction? Discuss the trade-offs.
questions.answer: A transaction should span exactly one unit of business work — typically one use case in the application layer, opened as late and closed as early as possible. Wrapping the entire request (an open-session-in-view style filter) keeps a connection and its locks held while you render a response or call a third-party API, which exhausts the pool and stretches lock windows until throughput collapses; it also masks lazy-loading bugs by letting the ORM fetch inside the view. Never perform external I/O — HTTP calls, emails, queue publishes — inside a transaction, because a rollback cannot undo them and a remote timeout holds your locks; use the transactional outbox pattern instead so the event is written in the same transaction and published after commit. Where a request genuinely spans several services, use a saga with compensating actions rather than a distributed transaction.
followUps: How does the transactional outbox guarantee at-least-once delivery?
Where do you put the transaction boundary in a DDD layered architecture?

questions.question: What is an ORM, and what are its main pitfalls in a production backend?
questions.answer: An ORM maps rows to objects and generates SQL, saving boilerplate for CRUD and giving you identity map, change tracking, and unit of work. The pitfalls: lazy loading producing N+1 queries (fix with explicit eager fetch/JOIN or a batch size, and assert query counts in tests); a leaky abstraction where the object model dictates bad SQL and you cannot express window functions, CTEs, or index hints without dropping to raw SQL anyway; implicit cascades and dirty-checking flushes that write when you did not expect it; and accidental full-table loads because a collection was iterated. The workable stance is to use the ORM for aggregate-shaped writes and simple reads, and hand-written SQL (or a query builder) for reporting and hot read paths — a CQRS-ish split — while always logging generated SQL in development.
followUps: How would you detect an N+1 regression automatically?
What does the identity map save you, and when does it hurt?

questions.question: Your team lets the ORM auto-generate migrations and applies them on application startup. What can go wrong, and what would you do instead?
questions.answer: Auto-generated migrations produce whatever DDL reconciles the model diff — often a blocking ALTER TABLE, a non-concurrent index build, or a DROP COLUMN that silently destroys data, and the diff can be non-deterministic between developers' local states. Running them at startup is worse: with several replicas rolling out, multiple instances race on the same DDL, a long migration blocks the readiness probe until the orchestrator kills the pod mid-migration, and a rollback of the deployment does not roll back the schema. Instead, treat migrations as reviewed, checked-in, hand-edited SQL under a versioned tool (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, golang-migrate) with an advisory lock, run them as a separate pipeline step or Kubernetes Job before the app rollout, keep them additive and backward compatible per the expand/contract rule, and test them against a production-sized copy to measure lock time before they touch prod.
followUps: How would you add a NOT NULL column to a 100M-row table without downtime?
How do you coordinate migrations across several services sharing a database?

questions.question: What is a monolith, and what does 'modular monolith' add on top of it?
questions.answer: A monolith is one deployable unit: a single process/artifact containing all features, with one database and in-process calls between modules. A modular monolith keeps that single deployment but enforces internal module boundaries — each module owns its tables, exposes a narrow public API (interfaces/facades), and cross-module access goes through that API rather than direct table joins or internal classes. Enforcement is done with package-private visibility, build modules (Gradle/Maven submodules, .NET projects, Go internal/ packages) or ArchUnit-style tests. You get single-transaction simplicity and one deploy, while keeping the seams that would later allow extraction.
followUps: How would you mechanically enforce that module A cannot import module B's internals?
What is the first thing that breaks module boundaries in practice?

questions.question: Name three concrete signs that splitting a system into microservices is the wrong decision right now.
questions.answer: First, the domain boundaries are still unstable — if you cannot name the bounded contexts and their invariants, every split will cut through an aggregate and produce chatty, distributed transactions. Second, the team is small (say under ~15 engineers): you pay for CI/CD per service, per-service on-call, service discovery, tracing and schema versioning without gaining independent deployability. Third, the real bottleneck is a single hot path (one slow query, one CPU-bound endpoint) — that is solved by an index, a cache or vertical scaling, not by a network hop. The honest test: if you cannot deploy the monolith independently per module today because of process, microservices will not fix the process.
followUps: What would you do instead as a first step?
Which metric would tell you the split is now justified?

questions.question: What is a bounded context, and how does it relate to a microservice?
questions.answer: A bounded context is a DDD boundary inside which a term has exactly one meaning and one model — 'Customer' in Billing (tax id, invoices) is a different model from 'Customer' in Support (tickets, SLA). Integration between contexts happens through explicit contracts: published events, an anti-corruption layer that translates the foreign model, or a shared kernel that both teams co-own. A microservice should never be smaller than one aggregate and is usually one bounded context or a slice of it; deploying two contexts in one service is fine, but splitting one aggregate across two services forces distributed transactions. Context mapping (upstream/downstream, customer-supplier, conformist) is what tells you which direction the dependency is allowed to point.
followUps: When is an anti-corruption layer worth the extra code?
Can two bounded contexts share a database schema?

questions.question: Describe DDD layering (domain / application / infrastructure / interfaces) and the dependency rule.
questions.answer: Domain holds entities, value objects, aggregates and domain services — pure business rules with no framework, no SQL, no HTTP. Application holds use cases: it orchestrates aggregates, opens the transaction, and calls ports (interfaces) it declares itself. Infrastructure implements those ports — repositories over JPA/SQL, message publishers, HTTP clients. Interfaces/adapters is the delivery edge: controllers, CLI, consumers, which map DTOs to commands. The dependency rule is one-directional and inward: infrastructure and interfaces depend on application and domain, never the reverse; the domain compiles without any of them, which is exactly what makes domain unit tests fast and framework-free.
followUps: Where does an ORM entity annotation belong under this rule?
How do you invert the dependency for a repository?

questions.question: Why is two-phase commit (2PC) rarely used across microservices, and what replaces it?
questions.answer: 2PC gives atomicity via a coordinator (prepare → commit), but participants hold locks for the whole round trip, and if the coordinator dies after prepare the participants are blocked in-doubt until it recovers — availability drops to the product of all participants' availability. It also requires XA support, which HTTP APIs, Kafka and most SaaS backends do not offer. The replacement is a saga: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event, with a compensating transaction per step (refund for charge, release for reserve) instead of rollback. Sagas trade atomicity for eventual consistency, so the business must accept intermediate states like 'order pending payment'.
followUps: Which steps cannot be compensated, and how do you order them?
Choreography or orchestration for a 6-step saga?

questions.question: Your service writes a row to Postgres and then publishes a Kafka event. Occasionally the DB row exists but no event was published. Diagnose and fix it.
questions.answer: That is the dual-write problem: the commit and the publish are two separate non-atomic operations, so a crash or broker timeout between them loses the event (and publishing before the commit can produce a phantom event for a rolled-back row). Fix with the transactional outbox: in the same DB transaction as the business write, INSERT into an `outbox` table (aggregate_id, type, payload, created_at); a relay — a poller with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or CDC via Debezium reading the WAL — publishes rows to Kafka and marks them sent. Delivery is then at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent, keyed on the outbox row's event id (an inbox/dedup table or an upsert). Order per aggregate is preserved by partitioning Kafka on aggregate_id.
followUps: Why SKIP LOCKED rather than a plain SELECT for the relay?
How do you keep the outbox table from growing unbounded?

questions.question: A product manager says 'the inventory count on the product page is wrong for a few seconds after an order'. Is this a bug?
questions.answer: Not necessarily — it is the expected behaviour of eventual consistency: the write went to the Orders service, an event propagates to the read model, and the projection lags by the queue delay. It is a bug only against a stated guarantee, so the real answer is to pin the SLO: e.g. 99% of projections applied within 2s, measured as event-timestamp to projection-commit lag, alerted on consumer lag. Where staleness is unacceptable (the decrement that decides oversell), you move that invariant inside one aggregate and one transaction rather than relying on a projection. For the UI, read-your-writes can be given by routing the user's own reads to the primary or by returning the optimistic value after their own write.
followUps: How do you measure projection lag end to end?
What breaks if two projections apply events out of order?

questions.question: What does a service mesh give you that a resilience library (Resilience4j, Polly, Hystrix) does not, and what is the cost?
questions.answer: A mesh (Istio, Linkerd) runs a sidecar proxy — or an ambient/node proxy — beside every pod and takes over L7 concerns outside the process: mTLS with automatic cert rotation and SPIFFE identities, retries/timeouts/outlier detection, traffic shifting for canaries (90/10 by weight, header-based routing), and uniform RED metrics plus trace headers, all applied identically to Java, Go and Python services without a code change. A library gives the same retries and circuit breaking but only for languages it supports, needs a redeploy to change policy, and cannot enforce mTLS between services it does not own. The cost is real: extra hop latency (typically sub-millisecond to a few ms p99), per-pod memory/CPU, a control plane to run and upgrade, and much harder debugging — a 503 may now come from Envoy, not your app.
followUps: How would you tell an Envoy-generated 503 from an application 503?
When is a mesh overkill for 5 services?

questions.question: What is a sidecar proxy, in concrete terms of how traffic reaches it?
questions.answer: It is a second container in the same pod, sharing the pod's network namespace and localhost with the app. An init container (or a CNI plugin) installs iptables REDIRECT rules so that all inbound and outbound TCP traffic of the pod is diverted to the proxy's ports (Envoy's 15006 inbound / 15001 outbound in Istio), so the application dials a plain hostname and never knows it was intercepted. The proxy then does service discovery from the control plane, applies routing/retry/mTLS policy, and forwards to the peer's sidecar. Practical consequences: the app must start tolerating the proxy not being ready yet, and the sidecar must be shut down last or in-flight requests on pod termination fail.
followUps: Why do batch Jobs hang when they finish before the sidecar exits?
What does ambient mode change about this?

questions.question: What causes serverless cold starts, and how do you reduce them without paying for idle?
questions.answer: A cold start happens when no warm execution environment exists: the platform must fetch and unpack the deployment artifact, boot the sandbox (Firecracker microVM for Lambda), start the runtime, and run your init code — the last part dominates for JVM/.NET and for anything doing DI scanning or TLS handshakes at import time. Reduce it by shrinking the package, moving SDK/DB client creation into init (reused across invocations) rather than per request, lazy-loading rarely used modules, and choosing a lighter runtime (Go/Node) or ahead-of-time compilation (GraalVM native image, .NET ReadyToRun). Platform levers: SnapStart (restores a pre-initialized snapshot), provisioned concurrency (costs money when idle) and higher memory settings, since memory also buys CPU and cuts init time. Cold starts also spike on scale-out and after every deploy, so they show up as p99 latency, not p50.
followUps: Why does raising memory from 512MB to 1769MB often halve cold start?
How do you measure cold start share of traffic?

questions.question: Why must a serverless function be stateless, and where does state actually live?
questions.answer: Because the platform can create, freeze, reuse or destroy an execution environment at any time and routes each invocation to an arbitrary instance — in-memory state and local disk (/tmp) survive only by luck for warm reuse, and never across instances. So session data goes to Redis/DynamoDB, uploaded files to S3, long-running work to a queue plus a state machine (Step Functions), and locks/counters to a store with conditional writes. What you may legitimately keep in the module scope is idempotent, derivable state: DB connection or SDK clients, parsed config, a small TTL'd cache — with the caveat that a pooled DB connection per instance multiplies by concurrency and can exhaust Postgres, which is why RDS Proxy or a serverless-friendly pooler exists.
followUps: What breaks if you cache a user's data in module scope?
How do you bound DB connections from 500 concurrent functions?

questions.question: A Lambda behind SQS suddenly scales to 800 concurrent executions, the RDS instance hits max_connections, and the bill triples. What do you change?
questions.answer: Serverless auto-scaling turns a traffic spike into a stampede against a non-elastic downstream, so you must cap concurrency, not the database. Set reserved concurrency on the function (e.g. 50) — SQS then simply keeps messages queued instead of amplifying — and tune the event source mapping's maximum concurrency and batch size so fewer invocations do more work per call. Put RDS Proxy (or PgBouncer) in front of Postgres so 50 executions share a small pool, and make handlers idempotent since SQS is at-least-once and throttled batches get redelivered. On cost: serverless is priced per GB-second plus per-request, so it wins for spiky and low-duty-cycle traffic and loses badly against a always-busy container — if the function runs near 100% of the time, a right-sized ECS/K8s deployment is cheaper, and that is the migration to propose.
followUps: Where do throttled messages end up, and how do you avoid silent loss?
At what utilization does the cost crossover happen for your workload?

questions.question: State the Twelve-Factor rules on config and backing services, and what violating them looks like in code.
questions.answer: Config (factor III) is everything that varies between deploys — credentials, hostnames, feature toggles — and it lives in environment variables, not in code and not in a checked-in `application-prod.yml`; the test is 'could this repo be open-sourced right now without leaking secrets?'. Backing services (factor IV) are attached resources reached only through a URL/credentials in config, so swapping a local Postgres for RDS, or a local file store for S3, is a config change with no code change. Violations look like `if (env == "prod") host = "db-prod.internal"` branching inside the app, a hardcoded connection string, or a per-environment build artifact — which also breaks factor V (build once, run the same artifact everywhere). In practice env vars come from Kubernetes Secrets/Vault/SSM injected at start, and the app fails fast at boot when a required variable is missing.
followUps: How do you handle 200 config values without a 200-line env block?
Why is failing fast on missing config better than a default?

questions.question: Explain the twelve-factor rules on disposability and logs, and why both matter in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: Disposability (factor IX) means processes start fast and shut down gracefully: on SIGTERM stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests within the grace period, and return unacknowledged queue messages so another worker picks them up. In Kubernetes that maps to terminationGracePeriodSeconds, a readiness probe that starts failing before the process dies (and usually a preStop sleep so endpoints are deregistered first) — without it, every rollout causes a burst of 502s. Logs (factor XI) are an event stream: the app writes plain unbuffered events to stdout/stderr and never manages files, rotation or shipping; the platform (kubectl logs → Fluent Bit → Loki/ELK) does routing. Emit structured JSON with a trace/request id so lines from many replicas can be correlated — with a dozen pods, grep on a local file is useless.
followUps: What order do readiness failure, SIGTERM and endpoint removal actually happen in?
Why is writing to a log file inside a container harmful?

questions.question: Walk through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF with a concrete example.
questions.answer: 1NF: atomic column values and no repeating groups — `phones = '555-1,555-2'` or columns `item1,item2,item3` violate it; split into rows in a child table. 2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key — in `OrderLine(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name)`, `product_name` depends only on `product_id`, so it moves to `Product`. 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency of a non-key on another non-key — `Employee(id, dept_id, dept_name)` must drop `dept_name` to the `Department` table. BCNF is the stricter form: every determinant must be a candidate key; the classic violation is `Enrollment(student, course, instructor)` where an instructor teaches exactly one course, so `instructor → course` holds although `instructor` is not a key, and the fix is to decompose into `(instructor, course)` and `(student, instructor)`.
followUps: Which anomaly (insert/update/delete) does each form eliminate?
Can a BCNF decomposition lose a functional dependency?

questions.question: When is denormalization the right call, and how do you keep the duplicated data from drifting?
questions.answer: When a read-heavy path pays too much for joins or aggregates that a normalized schema recomputes constantly: a feed joining 6 tables at 10k rps, a dashboard summing a billion rows, or a report needing a value that is historically frozen. The typical moves are a precomputed counter (`post.comment_count`), a materialized view refreshed on a schedule or CONCURRENTLY, a JSONB blob for the rendered object, or a read model in Elasticsearch fed by events. Crucially, some 'duplication' is not denormalization at all — an order line must store `unit_price` at purchase time, because the price is a fact of the order, not of the product. Keep the copies honest with a single writer plus a mechanism: triggers or an application-level update inside the same transaction, event-driven projection with a reconciliation job that recomputes and diffs nightly, and a monitored staleness metric. Denormalize only after measuring, since you trade write amplification and anomaly risk for read latency.
followUps: Trigger or application code for maintaining a counter — which and why?
How would you detect drift before a customer does?

questions.question: One downstream service slows from 50ms to 4s, and within two minutes every service in the cluster is unhealthy. Explain the mechanism and the fixes.
questions.answer: This is a cascading failure driven by thread/connection exhaustion: callers hold a worker per in-flight request, a 4s latency multiplies concurrency by ~80x (Little's Law: L = λ × W), the caller's pool fills, its own callers time out, and the failure walks up the graph. Retries make it worse — a retry storm with 3 attempts triples load exactly when the dependency is weakest, and synchronized client-side retries produce a thundering herd on recovery. Fixes: aggressive per-call timeouts smaller than the caller's own deadline (and deadline propagation so the whole chain gives up together), a circuit breaker that trips on error/slow-call rate and fails fast, bulkheads so one dependency gets its own bounded thread pool, retry budgets (retry only if retries are <10% of traffic) with exponential backoff plus full jitter, and load shedding at the edge returning 429/503 early. Long-term, the call should be asynchronous or the response degraded (cached/default value) rather than blocking.
followUps: How do you pick the timeout value — from which percentile?
Why full jitter rather than plain exponential backoff?

questions.question: What is a gray failure, and why do health checks miss it?
questions.answer: A gray failure is degraded-but-not-dead behaviour: the process answers /health with 200 because the check only proves the HTTP thread is alive, while real requests are slow, one shard or one AZ is failing, GC pauses are 2s, or a disk returns errors on 5% of writes. The system's internal view (up) differs from the observer's view (unusable), so the load balancer keeps sending traffic and nothing fails over — the classic 'differential observability' problem. Detect it with deep health checks that touch real dependencies, with client-side success/latency metrics rather than server-side liveness, outlier detection that ejects hosts whose error rate deviates from peers, and per-AZ/per-instance percentile dashboards instead of fleet averages, which hide a single bad node. Automatic remediation is typically eject-and-replace, plus enough capacity headroom that removing a suspect host is safe.
followUps: What's the risk of making liveness probes deep?
How do you avoid ejecting the whole fleet when the dependency itself is down?

questions.question: A Kafka consumer group stops making progress; lag grows and the same offset is reprocessed forever. What happened and what is the fix?
questions.answer: A poison pill: one message that always fails deserialization or processing (bad schema, null field, oversized payload), so the consumer throws, never commits the offset, rebalances or restarts, and re-reads the same record in an infinite loop — blocking every later message in that partition. Fix operationally by identifying the offset (consumer logs plus `kafka-consumer-groups --describe`) and either fixing the code or seeking past it with `--reset-offsets --shift-by 1` for that partition. Fix structurally: bound retries per record, then route the failure to a dead-letter topic with the original headers, error and stack trace, and commit the offset; add an ErrorHandlingDeserializer so malformed bytes become a marker rather than an exception, enforce compatibility with a schema registry, and alert on DLQ rate so failures are visible instead of silent. Then build the DLQ replay tool — a DLQ nobody can reprocess is just a landfill.
followUps: Why does one poison pill block only one partition, not the topic?
How do you preserve ordering after replaying from a DLQ?

questions.question: A cache key with a 1-hour TTL expires and the database instantly gets 20k identical queries. Name the pattern and the mitigations.
questions.answer: That is a thundering herd / cache stampede on a hot key (the 'dogpile' effect): every concurrent request misses simultaneously and all recompute the same value. Mitigations: single-flight — first miss takes a short-lived lock (`SET key:lock NX PX 5000`) or a per-key in-process mutex, and the others wait briefly or serve the stale value; probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), where a request refreshes before the TTL with probability rising as expiry approaches; background refresh-ahead for known hot keys; and serve-stale-while-revalidate so a miss never reaches the DB synchronously. Add jitter to TTLs (3600 ± 300s) so a batch of keys populated together does not expire together, which is the same herd at fleet scale — and note that a cold restart or cache flush produces the same spike, so warm the cache before shifting traffic.
followUps: What TTL jitter distribution would you pick and why?
How does this differ from cache penetration on a nonexistent key?

questions.question: An endpoint has p50 of 40ms and p99 of 3s. How do you find the cause, and why is averaging useless here?
questions.answer: The average hides a bimodal distribution — 40ms of real work plus a rare 3s stall — so you work on the tail directly: look at the p99 histogram, then use distributed tracing filtered to slow traces to see which span owns the time (DB, downstream call, queue wait, lock). Typical tail causes are GC pauses, a cold cache or cold start, connection-pool wait (queueing, not service time), a lock held across I/O, an N+1 that only triggers for large accounts, or one slow shard. Then profile the right dimension: a CPU flame graph (perf/async-profiler/pprof) if CPU is saturated, a wall-clock or off-CPU profile if the thread is blocked — a CPU profile shows nothing for a thread waiting on a socket. Fix by attacking the queue (pool size, concurrency limits), not just the code, since at high utilization latency is dominated by waiting.
followUps: Why can p99 rise while p50 is flat as load increases?
How do you tell GC pause from pool wait in a trace?

questions.question: How do you read a flame graph, and how do CPU, allocation and lock-contention profiles differ?
questions.answer: In a flame graph the x-axis is the share of collected samples (not time order, and the alphabetical ordering is meaningless), the y-axis is stack depth, and width equals cost — so you look for wide frames near the top, which are the leaves actually burning the resource; a wide bottom frame is just a common caller. A CPU profile samples on-CPU stacks and answers 'what is the processor executing'. An allocation profile samples by bytes allocated (async-profiler `-e alloc`, Go's `heap`/`allocs`) and finds GC pressure — code that is cheap on CPU but forces collections. A lock-contention/off-CPU profile (`-e lock`, `block`/`mutex` profiles, wall-clock mode) shows time threads spend blocked on monitors or I/O, which never appears in a CPU profile at all. Choosing the wrong one is the classic mistake: a service at 15% CPU and 4s latency needs the off-CPU view, not a CPU flame graph.
followUps: What is a differential flame graph used for?
Why is the JVM's safepoint bias a problem for sampling profilers?

questions.question: Your load test reports p99 = 120ms but production users see seconds. What is coordinated omission and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer: Coordinated omission happens when the load generator sends the next request only after the previous response arrives (closed-loop). When the server stalls for 2s, the generator simply stops issuing requests, so the many slow requests that would have occurred during the stall are never measured — one 2s sample replaces hundreds, and the tail is silently deleted. Avoid it by testing open-loop against a fixed arrival rate and measuring latency from the request's intended send time, not from when it was actually dispatched: wrk2, Gatling's constantUsersPerSec / injection profiles, k6 with constant-arrival-rate, or HdrHistogram's `recordValueWithExpectedInterval`. Also drop averages in favour of full histograms with p99/p99.9, and sanity-check against real production RUM percentiles, since a test whose throughput drops when the server slows down is measuring the server's permission to be slow.
followUps: Why does an open-loop test require queue/backpressure handling in the client?
How do you pick the target arrival rate?

questions.question: How would you migrate a large legacy monolith to services with a strangler-fig approach, and where do the API gateway and a BFF fit?
questions.answer: Put a facade — gateway or reverse proxy — in front of the monolith so all traffic is routable, then move one capability at a time: build the new service, dual-write or replicate its data, shift a small percentage of traffic by route with the old path as fallback, compare results (shadow traffic / diff testing), then cut over and delete the monolith code so the branch does not live forever. Order the slices by value and independence — a leaf capability with few writes first, never the shared core entity first — and keep every step reversible with a feature flag. The API gateway is the single edge concern: TLS termination, authn, rate limiting, routing and request aggregation shared by all clients. A BFF is one gateway per client type (web, iOS, partner API) owned by that client's team, shaping and aggregating responses for that UI — it exists so a mobile screen needing 5 services makes one call with the fields it needs, instead of bloating a shared gateway with client-specific logic. The risk is BFF proliferation and duplicated cross-cutting logic, so authn/rate limiting stay in the shared edge, and only shaping lives in the BFF.
followUps: How do you split the shared database during the strangle?
What tells you a slice is done and the old code can be deleted?
