questions.question: What is the difference between a queue-based broker like RabbitMQ and a log-based broker like Kafka?
questions.answer: RabbitMQ is a smart broker with dumb consumers: a message is routed into a queue, delivered to one consumer, acked, and then deleted, so the broker tracks per-message state. Kafka is a dumb broker with smart consumers: producers append to an immutable partitioned log, messages stay for the whole retention period, and each consumer group just stores an offset pointer. That means Kafka supports replay and many independent readers of the same data, while RabbitMQ supports rich routing, per-message TTL, priorities and selective redelivery that a log cannot express.
followUps: Which one would you pick for a task queue with 30-minute jobs?
Why can't you easily do per-message retry with backoff in Kafka?

questions.question: Explain RabbitMQ exchange types and how routing works.
questions.answer: Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key, never directly to a queue; bindings connect exchanges to queues. A direct exchange matches routing key exactly, fanout ignores the key and copies to every bound queue, topic matches patterns with * (one word) and # (zero or more words) such as order.*.created, and headers matches on header attributes instead of the key. A message that matches no binding is dropped silently unless the exchange has an alternate-exchange, or the publisher sets the mandatory flag and handles basic.return.
followUps: How do you detect messages being silently dropped?
When is a topic exchange better than several direct bindings?

questions.question: A RabbitMQ consumer processes messages fine but the queue keeps growing, and restarting the consumer causes thousands of messages to be reprocessed. What is going on?
questions.answer: Almost certainly the consumer subscribed with autoAck=false but never calls basic.ack, or it acks only after a long batch. Unacked messages count as delivered-but-outstanding, so they stay in the queue in the Unacked state and are requeued on channel close, which explains the reprocessing. Check the Unacked column in rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged; if unacked is large and stuck, fix the ack path and set a sane basic.qos prefetch so one consumer can't hold thousands of messages hostage.
followUps: What prefetch value would you start with for 50ms jobs vs 30s jobs?
What happens to unacked messages if the consumer process is SIGKILLed?

questions.question: How do you handle a poison message that fails every time it is consumed?
questions.answer: Never requeue it blindly with basic.nack(requeue=true) — that creates a hot loop that starves the queue. Instead count attempts (x-death header in RabbitMQ, or a custom attempt header), and after N failures reject with requeue=false so the queue's x-dead-letter-exchange routes it to a DLQ. A common pattern is a retry queue with per-message TTL that dead-letters back to the main queue for delayed retry with backoff, and a terminal DLQ that alerts a human. In Kafka the equivalent is a retry topic chain plus a dead-letter topic, because you cannot skip a single message without committing past it.
followUps: How do you replay a DLQ safely after a fix?
What metric tells you a poison loop is happening?

questions.question: What guarantees does Kafka give about message ordering?
questions.answer: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition, not across a topic. Messages with the same key hash to the same partition, so ordering per entity (per user id, per order id) is preserved if you key by that entity. Ordering also breaks if you set max.in.flight.requests.per.connection > 1 with retries and without enable.idempotence=true, because a retried batch can land after a later one. Increasing partition count later rehashes keys, so historical and future messages for one key can end up in different partitions.
followUps: How do you scale throughput when one key is extremely hot?
Why is adding partitions a semi-breaking change?

questions.question: Explain Kafka consumer groups, offsets, and rebalancing.
questions.answer: Within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so group parallelism is capped by partition count; extra consumers sit idle. Each consumer commits an offset per partition to the __consumer_offsets topic, and on restart it resumes from the last committed offset. When a member joins, leaves, or misses max.poll.interval.ms / session.timeout.ms, the group rebalances and partitions are reassigned — with the eager protocol everyone stops consuming briefly, which is why cooperative-sticky assignment and static group membership (group.instance.id) are preferred to avoid stop-the-world pauses during deploys.
followUps: Why does slow processing cause repeated rebalances?
What does auto.offset.reset=earliest vs latest change on a brand new group?

questions.question: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, and how you make a consumer idempotent.
questions.answer: At-most-once commits the offset/ack before processing, so a crash loses messages; at-least-once processes then commits, so a crash replays and duplicates; exactly-once requires the read-process-write to be atomic. Kafka offers exactly-once-semantics for Kafka-to-Kafka flows via the idempotent producer plus transactions and isolation.level=read_committed, but the moment you write to an external database or call a payment API you are back to at-least-once end-to-end. The practical answer is at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer: derive a deterministic key from the message (event id, or entity id + version) and use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, a unique constraint on processed_events, or a conditional update guarded by a version number.
followUps: How long do you keep processed-event ids around?
Where does Kafka's exactly-once actually fail at the boundary?

questions.question: Consumer lag on one topic has grown to 40 million messages and is still climbing. Walk through your response.
questions.answer: First separate the causes: is production spiking, or is consumption slow? Look at per-partition lag (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe) — if lag is concentrated in a few partitions it is key skew or a stuck consumer, if it is uniform the group is simply under-provisioned. Check consumer-side metrics for processing time per record, downstream DB latency, and rebalance frequency, since a rebalance loop caused by max.poll.interval.ms timeouts halts progress entirely. Fixes in order: raise max.poll.records batching and use bulk writes downstream, add consumers up to the partition count, add partitions if already saturated, and if the backlog is stale or non-critical, shed load by seeking offsets forward after an explicit business decision.
followUps: How do you verify retention won't delete the backlog before you catch up?
When is seeking past a backlog acceptable?

questions.question: What is the difference between Kafka's time-based retention and log compaction?
questions.answer: cleanup.policy=delete drops whole log segments once retention.ms or retention.bytes is exceeded, which suits event streams where old events lose value. cleanup.policy=compact keeps at least the latest value per key forever, so the topic becomes a replayable snapshot of current state — used for changelog and CDC topics, and for Kafka Streams state stores. Compaction is asynchronous, so duplicates of a key can exist until the cleaner runs, and a delete is expressed as a tombstone (null value) which is itself removed after delete.retention.ms. You can also set compact,delete to bound the size of a compacted topic.
followUps: Why must compacted topics always have a non-null key?
How does a consumer that misses a tombstone end up with stale state?

questions.question: A service writes an order to Postgres and then publishes an OrderCreated event. Sometimes the DB row exists but no event was published. How do you fix it?
questions.answer: This is dual-write failure: the commit and the publish are not atomic, so a crash between them loses the event (and a publish-first design loses the row). Use the transactional outbox: in the same transaction that inserts the order, insert a row into an outbox table, then have a separate relay poll the outbox or tail the WAL via CDC (Debezium) and publish to the broker, marking rows sent. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent on the event id, and ordering is preserved if the relay reads the outbox in id/sequence order and keys by aggregate id.
followUps: Why is a two-phase commit between DB and broker usually rejected here?
What does the outbox relay do if the broker is down for an hour?

questions.question: What are Server-Sent Events and when would you choose them over a message broker consumer in the browser?
questions.answer: SSE is a long-lived HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream where the server pushes newline-delimited frames (data:, event:, id:, retry:) and the browser's EventSource reconnects automatically. It is one-directional server-to-client, text only, and runs over ordinary HTTP so proxies, auth cookies and HTTP/2 multiplexing work unchanged. Browsers cannot speak AMQP or the Kafka protocol, so the usual architecture is broker to backend, and backend fans out to browsers over SSE — SSE is the last hop, not a replacement for the broker.
followUps: What is the 6-connection-per-domain limit problem under HTTP/1.1?
How does the server tell the client to back off reconnecting?

questions.question: Your SSE stream works locally but through nginx clients receive nothing for 60 seconds and then the connection drops. Diagnose.
questions.answer: Two classic causes. nginx is buffering the response, so frames are held until a buffer fills — fix with proxy_buffering off (or send the X-Accel-Buffering: no response header) and proxy_http_version 1.1. The drop at 60s is proxy_read_timeout, whose default is 60s: either raise it for the SSE location or, better, emit a heartbeat comment line (`: ping\n\n`) every 15-30s, which also keeps corporate proxies and load balancer idle timeouts from killing the stream. Also disable gzip on the stream location, since compression buffers, and confirm the app framework isn't buffering the response itself.
followUps: Why is a comment line a good heartbeat rather than a real event?
How does the client resume after such a drop?

questions.question: How does Last-Event-ID work and what must the server do to support resume?
questions.answer: If the server includes `id: <n>` in frames, EventSource remembers the last one and on automatic reconnect sends it in the Last-Event-ID request header (the retry: field sets the reconnect delay in ms). The server must read that header and replay everything after that id, which means it needs a bounded, ordered per-stream buffer — a Redis stream, a Kafka offset, or a DB sequence — not just in-memory state on one instance, or a reconnect that lands on another pod loses events. Define behaviour when the id is older than the buffer: send a resync/snapshot event rather than silently starting from now.
followUps: How do you keep ids monotonic across multiple producing instances?
What's the memory cost of the replay buffer at 100k connections?

questions.question: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
questions.answer: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and acts on their behalf — corporate egress filtering, caching, or hiding the client's IP from the origin; the client is configured to use it. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts on their behalf — the client thinks it is talking to the origin, and the proxy handles TLS termination, load balancing, caching, compression, rate limiting and routing to upstreams. nginx, Caddy, HAProxy and Envoy are typically deployed as reverse proxies; Squid is the classic forward proxy.

questions.question: Explain nginx's worker and event model and why it scales better than a thread-per-connection server.
questions.answer: nginx runs one master process (reads config, binds ports, spawns workers) and N worker processes, typically worker_processes auto to match CPU cores, each pinned to a core. Each worker is single-threaded and handles thousands of connections in a non-blocking event loop using epoll on Linux or kqueue on BSD, so memory per connection is a few KB rather than a whole thread stack. Capacity is roughly worker_processes × worker_connections, and since a proxied request uses one connection to the client and one to the upstream, effective client capacity is about half that. The trade-off: any blocking operation in a worker stalls every connection it holds, which is why disk I/O uses thread pools (aio threads) and why nginx doesn't embed application code.

questions.question: Users report intermittent 502 and 504 errors from nginx. How do you tell them apart and debug?
questions.answer: 502 Bad Gateway means nginx reached the upstream but the response was invalid or the connection was refused/reset — the app crashed, the socket is wrong, or the worker died mid-request. 504 Gateway Timeout means nginx waited longer than proxy_read_timeout (default 60s) for the response, or proxy_connect_timeout (default 60s, capped by the OS) to establish it. Read error.log, which names the upstream and the exact reason (connect() failed, upstream prematurely closed connection), and add $upstream_addr, $upstream_status and $upstream_response_time to log_format so you can see which backend and how long. Common fixes: raise upstream keepalive and set proxy_http_version 1.1 with Connection "" to avoid churning connections, align nginx timeouts with the app's own timeouts, and increase the app's listen backlog or worker count if it is simply saturated.
followUps: Why can a keepalive race cause sporadic 502s?
Should you raise proxy_read_timeout or fix the slow endpoint?

questions.question: How do upstream health checks work in nginx, and what is the difference between passive and active checks?
questions.answer: Open-source nginx does passive checks only: within an upstream block, max_fails (default 1) and fail_timeout (default 10s) mark a server unavailable after that many failed real requests, and it is retried after fail_timeout. proxy_next_upstream controls which conditions (error, timeout, http_502, http_503) cause a retry on another server, bounded by proxy_next_upstream_tries and _timeout. Active out-of-band probing (health_check with an interval and a match block) is an nginx Plus feature; on OSS you use a separate LB, HAProxy, or Envoy for that. Never put non-idempotent conditions like http_500 on POST retries without thinking, because proxy_next_upstream will replay the request.

questions.question: What does nginx proxy buffering do, and when should you turn it off?
questions.answer: With proxy_buffering on (the default), nginx reads the whole upstream response into proxy_buffers (spilling to disk past proxy_max_temp_file_size) and only then streams it to the client. That frees the application worker immediately, which matters hugely for slow clients — an app process isn't held hostage by a mobile user on 2G. Turn it off only for streaming responses: SSE, chunked progress output, large downloads generated on the fly, and WebSocket-adjacent endpoints, where buffering adds latency or breaks the stream entirely. The mirror setting is client_body_buffering for uploads, and client_max_body_size, whose 1m default is the usual cause of 413 on file uploads.

questions.question: What is TLS termination and what are the trade-offs of terminating at the edge?
questions.answer: TLS termination means the proxy decrypts HTTPS and forwards plaintext HTTP to upstreams; it centralizes certificates, enables HTTP-level routing, caching and compression, and offloads handshake CPU from app servers. The cost is that traffic behind the proxy is unencrypted, which fails many compliance regimes, so you either re-encrypt (TLS passthrough or proxy_pass to https:// upstreams, i.e. TLS bridging) or run a service mesh with mTLS. When terminating, the app loses the client's identity, so the proxy must set X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and Host, and the app must trust those headers only from the proxy's IP or an attacker can spoof them. Also enable HTTP/2 and OCSP stapling at the edge and keep session resumption on to cut handshake cost.
followUps: How does an app get tricked by a spoofed X-Forwarded-Proto?
When is TLS passthrough required?

questions.question: How does Caddy's automatic HTTPS work, and when would you choose Caddy over nginx?
questions.answer: Caddy provisions and renews certificates automatically from Let's Encrypt/ZeroSSL using ACME — HTTP-01 or TLS-ALPN-01 by default, DNS-01 via a provider module for wildcards — simply because a site address in the Caddyfile is a public hostname; it redirects HTTP to HTTPS, staples OCSP and renews at ~2/3 of the certificate lifetime with no cron or certbot. It also stores certificates in a shared storage backend so a cluster does not hit rate limits. Choose Caddy when you want secure-by-default TLS with minimal config, an HTTP/3 default and a clean config language; choose nginx when you need its maturity, raw throughput at very high connection counts, or the huge ecosystem of existing modules and configuration knowledge.

questions.question: Explain Apache's prefork, worker and event MPMs and which to use.
questions.answer: prefork spawns one single-threaded process per connection — highest memory per connection but process isolation, and the only safe choice for non-thread-safe modules like classic mod_php. worker is hybrid: several processes each with many threads, so far less memory per connection, but a thread is still occupied for the whole keep-alive period. event extends worker by handing idle keep-alive connections to a dedicated listener thread, so threads are only held while a request is actually being processed — the correct default for modern Apache. The usual modern deployment is event MPM plus PHP-FPM over proxy_fcgi, which decouples request handling from the application runtime entirely.

What does MaxRequestWorkers actually cap?

questions.question: An Apache server under load shows most memory consumed and requests queuing, but CPU is only 30%. What is likely wrong?
questions.answer: Classic prefork MPM exhaustion: each connection is a full process at 20-80MB with modules loaded, so MaxRequestWorkers is reached long before CPU saturates and new connections sit in the listen backlog. Check `apachectl -V` for the MPM in use, server-status for busy vs idle workers, and per-process RSS. Fixes: move to the event MPM with PHP-FPM, strip unused loaded modules to shrink the process image, lower KeepAliveTimeout (5s, not the old 15s) so workers aren't parked on idle connections, and put static assets behind nginx or a CDN so Apache workers aren't spent serving files. Raising MaxRequestWorkers without more RAM just converts queuing into swapping, which is worse.
followUps: How do you compute a safe MaxRequestWorkers from RSS and RAM?
Why is swapping worse than queuing here?

questions.question: How do you configure gzip and Brotli compression correctly at the edge?
questions.answer: Compress only text-like types (text/html, text/css, application/javascript, application/json, image/svg+xml) and never already-compressed formats — JPEG, PNG, WebP, MP4, zip — because re-compressing burns CPU for nothing. Set gzip_min_length around 1024 since tiny bodies can grow, keep gzip_comp_level moderate (4-6) because level 9 costs far more CPU for ~2% gain, and add gzip_vary on so caches key on Accept-Encoding. Brotli (ngx_brotli, built into Caddy) gives roughly 15-20% smaller text than gzip at similar speed and is preferred by browsers over HTTPS; the best pattern is precompressed static files (brotli_static/gzip_static at level 11) plus dynamic gzip for API responses. Disable compression on SSE and other streaming endpoints, and be aware of BREACH when compressing responses that mix secrets with reflected user input.
followUps: Why does a missing Vary header poison a shared cache?
When is precompression clearly better than on-the-fly?

questions.question: A login endpoint is being credential-stuffed. How do you rate limit at the edge in nginx?
questions.answer: Define a shared zone keyed by the real client IP — limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login:10m rate=5r/m; — and apply it in the login location with limit_req zone=login burst=5 nodelay, which uses a leaky bucket: burst allows a short spike and nodelay serves it immediately instead of queueing, returning 429 via limit_req_status 429 beyond that. Pair it with limit_conn to cap concurrent connections per IP. Key correctly: behind a CDN or LB, $binary_remote_addr is the proxy, so you need real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For with set_real_ip_from restricted to your trusted proxy CIDRs, otherwise the header is attacker-controlled. Edge rate limiting is necessary but not sufficient — distributed botnets rotate IPs, so also add per-account throttling, progressive delays and MFA in the application.

questions.question: What is Microsoft IIS and where does it still make sense?
questions.answer: IIS is the Windows web server, integrated with the OS: sites run in application pools, each pool a w3wp.exe worker process with its own identity, recycling rules and isolation, configured via applicationHost.config and per-site web.config with a modular pipeline. It makes sense for classic ASP.NET Framework applications, Windows/Active Directory integrated authentication (Kerberos/NTLM), and shops standardized on Windows Server tooling. For modern ASP.NET Core the runtime is Kestrel, with IIS acting as a reverse proxy via the ASP.NET Core Module — and many teams now put Kestrel behind nginx or a cloud load balancer on Linux instead, since .NET Core is cross-platform.
followUps: What does application pool recycling protect you from?
Why is Kestrel not exposed directly to the internet in older guidance?

questions.question: Your reverse proxy must serve a React SPA, a REST API, and a WebSocket endpoint on one domain. Sketch the nginx configuration decisions.
questions.answer: Three locations with different behaviour. Static: `location /` with try_files $uri /index.html so client-side routes resolve, long immutable Cache-Control for hashed assets and no-cache for index.html. API: `location /api/` with proxy_pass to the upstream, proxy_set_header Host/X-Real-IP/X-Forwarded-For/X-Forwarded-Proto, buffering on, and timeouts tuned to the slowest legitimate endpoint. WebSocket: `location /ws` with proxy_http_version 1.1, proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade and Connection "upgrade", proxy_read_timeout well above the heartbeat interval (e.g. 3600s), and buffering off. Add an upstream block with keepalive to reuse backend connections, gzip on text types only, and a shared TLS config at the server level with HTTP redirected to HTTPS.
followUps: Why does the Upgrade header need the map trick when keepalive is on?
How would the same setup look in a Caddyfile?

questions.question: What is graceful degradation, and when should a service fail closed instead?
questions.answer: Graceful degradation means shedding non-essential functionality so the core path keeps working: if the recommendation service times out, render the product page with a static fallback list instead of returning 500. It applies when the missing data is advisory. Fail closed when the dependency is a correctness or safety gate - payment authorization, permission checks, fraud scoring - where serving the request without it means money loss or a security hole. The rule of thumb: degrade on read-side enrichment, fail closed on authorization and money.
followUps: How do you cache a fallback response so degradation has something to serve?
Which HTTP status do you return for a degraded but successful response?

questions.question: Compare token bucket, leaky bucket and sliding window rate limiting.
questions.answer: Token bucket refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a capacity; a request consumes one token, so bursts up to the capacity are allowed - good for APIs that want smooth average rate with burst tolerance. Leaky bucket drains at a constant rate through a queue, producing perfectly smooth output and shaping traffic, but it delays instead of allowing bursts. Fixed-window counters are cheap but allow 2x the limit across a window boundary; sliding window log stores timestamps (exact, memory-heavy) and sliding window counter interpolates the previous window's count (approximate, O(1) memory) to fix the boundary problem.
followUps: Which headers do you return when throttling (X-RateLimit-*, Retry-After)?
Why is 429 preferred over 503 for a rate-limited caller?

questions.question: Design distributed rate limiting for 40 API nodes. Why Redis plus a Lua script?
questions.answer: Per-node limits do not compose: 40 nodes each allowing 100 rps means 4000 rps globally, and sticky routing breaks on rebalance. Centralize the counter in Redis keyed by tenant plus route, and run the check-and-decrement as a Lua script (EVALSHA) so read-modify-write is atomic on the server - otherwise GET then INCR races between nodes. A typical token-bucket script stores tokens and last_refill in a HASH, computes refill from redis TIME, decrements, sets a TTL, and returns allowed plus retry_after. Accept the added ~1ms hop, use a local in-process limiter as a fast pre-filter, and fail open (or fall back to a conservative local limit) if Redis is unreachable so the limiter is not itself an outage.
followUps: How do you shard the limiter keys to avoid a hot Redis slot?

questions.question: What is backpressure, and how is it expressed in queues versus streams?
questions.answer: Backpressure is the consumer telling the producer to slow down instead of silently buffering until memory or latency explodes. In streams it is explicit demand: TCP's receive window, HTTP/2 flow control, Reactive Streams request(n), or Node's writable.write() returning false plus the 'drain' event. In message queues it is indirect - you bound the queue, and when it is full you block the producer, reject with 429/503, or drop by priority; Kafka instead bounds consumer fetch (max.poll.records) and lets lag grow on durable storage. Unbounded queues are the anti-pattern: they convert a throughput problem into an unbounded latency problem and eventually an OOM.
followUps: Why does Little's Law say a bigger queue cannot fix an under-provisioned consumer?
How does a bounded thread pool with a rejection policy act as backpressure?

questions.question: Traffic triples during a flash sale and every request gets slow, including health checks. How do you shed load by priority?
questions.answer: Classify traffic before you shed it: checkout and payment callbacks are critical, search and product reads are important, analytics beacons and recommendation refreshes are droppable. At the edge, drop the lowest class first with 429/503 plus Retry-After once a signal crosses a threshold - CPU, or better, queue wait time / concurrency in flight (a Little's Law estimate of latency). Keep a reserved concurrency bulkhead for critical traffic and an admin/health path that is never shed, and shed early at the LB rather than after the request already consumed a DB connection. Shedding 20% fast beats letting 100% time out, because timed-out work still costs full capacity.
followUps: Why is queue-wait-time a better shed signal than CPU?
How do you avoid shedding a user's retry after already accepting their payment?

questions.question: Explain circuit breaker states and how half-open probing works.
questions.answer: Closed: calls pass, failures and slow calls are counted over a rolling window. When the failure ratio crosses a threshold (say 50% over the last 100 calls, with a minimum call volume so 2 of 2 does not trip it), it moves to Open and fails fast immediately - no connection, no timeout wait - for a cooldown like 30s. It then moves to Half-Open and admits a small fixed number of trial calls (e.g. 5, with concurrency capped); if they succeed it closes, if any fail it re-opens with a longer cooldown. Half-open must limit concurrency, otherwise the whole backlog stampedes the recovering dependency and immediately re-trips the breaker.
followUps: Why count slow calls, not only errors, toward tripping?
Should a 400 from the dependency count as a failure? Why not?

questions.question: A downstream service has a 10s blip, but your service stays down for 20 minutes afterwards. What happened and how do you fix the retry policy?
questions.answer: A retry storm: every client retried 3 times immediately and in lockstep, tripling load on a service that was already at the edge, and synchronized retries kept re-hammering it in waves. Fix with exponential backoff plus full jitter - sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)) - which spreads retries instead of aligning them. Add a retry budget (e.g. retries capped at 10% of requests, as in gRPC's retryThrottling), stop retrying non-idempotent or 4xx responses, honor Retry-After, and put a circuit breaker in front so retries stop entirely while the dependency is open. Also cap total attempts by a deadline, not a count.
followUps: Why is 'equal jitter' usually worse than full jitter?
How do layered retries at 3 tiers turn 3 attempts into 27?

questions.question: What is the bulkhead pattern and how do you implement it in a service?
questions.answer: Bulkheads partition resources so one saturated dependency cannot consume the whole process, named after ship compartments. Concretely: a separate bounded thread pool or semaphore per downstream (e.g. 20 permits for the search client, 50 for the DB), separate connection pools, and at infrastructure level separate instance groups or cells per tenant class. Without it, one slow dependency holds every request thread and the service becomes 100% unavailable even though 90% of its endpoints do not use that dependency. The cost is lower utilization and more tuning knobs, and permits must be sized from concurrency = throughput x latency.
followUps: Semaphore isolation vs thread-pool isolation - when is each right?
How do cell-based architectures extend bulkheads to blast radius?

questions.question: Design timeouts and deadline budgets across a 4-hop request chain.
questions.answer: Set a single deadline at the edge (say 2s), propagate the remaining budget on every hop (gRPC deadlines, or a header like grpc-timeout / X-Request-Deadline), and have each hop subtract its own elapsed time before calling the next. A hop must never set a timeout larger than its remaining budget, and each layer's timeout must be strictly shorter than its caller's, otherwise the caller gives up while the callee keeps burning capacity on work nobody will read. Base per-call timeouts on measured p99 plus headroom, not round numbers, and cancel downstream work when the deadline passes (context cancellation, closing the connection). Separate connect, TLS, and read timeouts - a missing read timeout is the classic cause of permanently hung pools.
followUps: What happens when retries are allowed inside a shared deadline budget?
How do you decide between hedged requests and a longer timeout?

questions.question: Define SLI, SLO and error budget with a worked example.
questions.answer: An SLI is a measured ratio of good events to valid events, e.g. the fraction of HTTP requests returning non-5xx in under 300ms. An SLO is the target on that SLI over a window, e.g. 99.9% over 28 days. The error budget is the allowed shortfall: 0.1% of 28 days is about 40 minutes of total unavailability, or 0.1% of requests. It turns reliability into a spendable resource - budget left means ship faster and run experiments; budget exhausted means freeze risky releases and work reliability. Alert on burn rate (e.g. page at 14.4x burn over 1h, which consumes 2% of a 30-day budget) rather than on every individual error spike.
followUps: Why should an SLO be below what you currently achieve, but not at 100%?

questions.question: Logs, metrics and traces - what does each answer, and where does OpenTelemetry fit?
questions.answer: Metrics are cheap pre-aggregated numeric time series that answer 'is something wrong and how much' (request rate, error ratio, p99) and drive alerts, but cannot explain a single request. Logs are high-cardinality discrete events that answer 'what exactly happened to this request', ideally structured JSON with a trace_id. Traces stitch spans across services with a trace context, answering 'where did the 900ms go' and revealing the dependency graph. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for all three: SDKs plus auto-instrumentation produce the data, W3C traceparent propagates context, and the Collector receives, processes (batching, tail sampling, attribute scrubbing) and exports to backends like Prometheus, Tempo or ClickHouse.

How do exemplars link a metric spike to a specific trace?

questions.question: Prometheus starts OOM-killing after a deploy and queries time out. Investigation shows 4 million active series. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: Cardinality explosion: someone added an unbounded label such as user_id, order_id, full URL path, or a raw error message to a metric. Total series is the product of all label value counts, so one label with a million values multiplies every other dimension. Diagnose with `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` and the /api/v1/status/tsdb cardinality endpoint. Fix by removing the unbounded label, templating the path (/users/{id}) before it becomes a label, moving per-entity detail to logs or traces where it belongs, and enforcing limits with metric_relabel_configs plus sample_limit / label limits so the next bad deploy is dropped at scrape time instead of taking the server down.
followUps: Why do histogram metrics multiply cardinality by the bucket count?
When is a high-cardinality store like ClickHouse a better fit than Prometheus?

questions.question: What are the RED and USE methods, and when do you use each?
questions.answer: RED is for request-driven services: Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec or ratio), Duration (latency distribution, p50/p90/p99 - never just the mean). It describes the user-visible symptom, so it drives SLOs and paging. USE is for resources: for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, connection pool, thread pool) track Utilization, Saturation (queue depth or wait time) and Errors. USE finds the cause once RED says there is a symptom - e.g. RED shows p99 at 3s, USE shows the DB connection pool at 100% utilization with a growing wait queue. Page on RED, diagnose with USE.
followUps: Why is saturation often a better early warning than utilization?
What are the Four Golden Signals and how do they map onto RED?

questions.question: You must store 50 TB of clickstream events for analytics, plus a low-latency per-user event feed, plus a social graph for 'friends of friends'. Which of ClickHouse, ScyllaDB and DGraph fits each, and why?
questions.answer: ClickHouse for the analytics: it is a columnar OLAP engine with a MergeTree primary-key sort order, per-column compression and vectorized execution, so scanning billions of rows for GROUP BY aggregates over a few columns is fast and cheap - but it is poor at single-row point updates and high-QPS point lookups. ScyllaDB for the per-user feed: it is a C++ Cassandra-compatible wide-column store with a shard-per-core (thread-per-core, shared-nothing) architecture pinned to cores with its own scheduler, giving predictable sub-millisecond p99 point reads by partition key at very high throughput - provided you model by query, since there are no joins and secondary indexes are limited. DGraph for the graph: multi-hop traversals like friends-of-friends are joins in SQL that explode combinatorially, while a native graph store follows adjacency lists directly and exposes a GraphQL-style query language. Do not force all three into one store; each is optimized for a different access pattern.
followUps: Why does ScyllaDB avoid the JVM GC pauses Cassandra suffers from?
How do ClickHouse materialized views pre-aggregate on insert?

questions.question: Compare short polling, long polling, SSE and WebSockets, and say when each fits.
questions.answer: Short polling requests on a fixed interval — simplest, but wastes requests and adds up to one interval of latency. Long polling holds the request open until data exists or a timeout fires, then the client immediately re-requests — near push latency over plain HTTP, but a held connection per client and an awkward gap between responses. SSE is a single persistent HTTP response for server-to-client pushes with built-in auto-reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume — ideal for notifications, feeds, progress bars and LLM token streaming. WebSockets upgrade to a full-duplex binary-capable TCP channel — the right choice only when the client also sends frequent messages, as in chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing or trading.
followUps: Which would you pick for a dashboard refreshed every 30s?
Why is SSE often preferred over WebSocket for one-way streams?

questions.question: How does the WebSocket handshake work?
questions.answer: The client sends a normal HTTP/1.1 GET with Connection: Upgrade, Upgrade: websocket, Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 and a random base64 Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept = base64(SHA1(key + 258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11)), after which the same TCP connection carries binary WebSocket frames instead of HTTP. ws:// is plain and wss:// runs over TLS; wss is effectively mandatory in production because intermediaries frequently mangle unencrypted upgrades.
