What does subprotocol negotiation via Sec-WebSocket-Protocol do?

questions.question: You scale your WebSocket chat service from 1 to 6 pods and users stop receiving each other's messages. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: Each pod holds only its own connections in local memory, so a message published on pod A never reaches a recipient connected to pod C. Fix by making the fan-out external: publish every message to Redis Pub/Sub, NATS, or a Kafka topic, and have each pod forward to the local sockets subscribed to that room. Separately, the HTTP upgrade must reach a pod that then keeps the connection, so the load balancer needs sticky/consistent routing or at least session affinity for reconnect-with-resume, and you must raise the LB and ingress idle timeout above your heartbeat interval.
followUps: Why is Redis Pub/Sub fire-and-forget a problem for message durability?
How do you avoid fanning a room message to all 6 pods when only one has members?

questions.question: Why do WebSocket connections need heartbeats, and how should reconnect be implemented?
questions.answer: TCP will not tell you about a silently dead peer, and NATs, load balancers and mobile networks drop idle connections after 30-120 seconds, so the server sends protocol-level ping frames (or app-level pings) every ~30s and closes the socket if no pong arrives within a timeout. Clients must reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter — without jitter a broker restart triggers a thundering herd where every client reconnects simultaneously. On reconnect, resume rather than restart: send the last received message id/sequence so the server replays the gap, and treat the connection as unreliable by making all message handling idempotent by message id.
followUps: Why measure liveness from the server side too, not only the client?
What backoff cap would you use for a 500k-client fleet?

questions.question: How do you authenticate and authorize a WebSocket connection?
questions.answer: The browser WebSocket API cannot set custom headers, so common options are a cookie sent with the handshake, a short-lived ticket token in the query string, or a first application-level auth message before any subscription is honoured. Validate at the handshake and reject with a 401/403 on the HTTP response rather than after the upgrade, and check the Origin header explicitly because WebSockets are not protected by the same-origin policy or CORS — that is the cross-site WebSocket hijacking (CSWSH) risk. Since the connection may live for hours, re-check authorization on sensitive actions and enforce a max session lifetime so a revoked token cannot keep streaming data.
followUps: Why is a long-lived JWT in the URL risky?
How do you kick a user whose permissions were just revoked?

questions.question: Implement long polling correctly — what are the failure modes?
questions.answer: The server holds the request until an event arrives or a timeout (typically 25-30s, below any proxy read timeout) and returns a cursor the client sends back on the next request. Failure modes: without a cursor, events produced in the gap between the response and the next request are lost; blocking threads per connection exhausts a thread-per-request server, so it needs async/event-driven handling; and intermediate proxies with a 60s read timeout or aggressive buffering break it. Also return 204/empty on timeout rather than an error, so client retry logic doesn't treat a normal timeout as a failure and back off.
followUps: What connection limits does HTTP/1.1 impose per origin?
How does HTTP/2 change the cost of long polling?

questions.question: A dashboard used by 20,000 users short-polls /api/stats every 2 seconds and the database is melting. How do you reduce load without losing freshness?
questions.answer: 20k clients at 0.5 rps is 10k rps hitting the DB for data that changes far less often. Put a short TTL cache in front (Redis or nginx proxy_cache with a 1-2s TTL and proxy_cache_lock on to collapse the stampede), so the DB sees roughly one query per TTL regardless of client count. Add ETag/Last-Modified so unchanged responses return 304 with no body, jitter the client interval to break synchronized waves, and back off the interval when the tab is hidden via the Page Visibility API. If freshness truly matters, switch the endpoint to SSE and push only on change — that converts 10k rps into one broadcast per actual update.
followUps: Why does a fixed interval create a synchronized thundering herd?
What breaks if you cache per-user data at the edge?

questions.question: What is Apache Solr and how does it differ from Elasticsearch?
questions.answer: Both are search engines built on Apache Lucene with inverted indexes, so core scoring (BM25), analyzers, tokenizers and near-real-time search behave similarly. Solr is older, uses ZooKeeper for SolrCloud coordination, favours an explicit schema (schema.xml / managed-schema) and has very strong faceting, and it is fully Apache-licensed. Elasticsearch has a JSON-first REST API, dynamic mapping by default, built-in coordination since 7.x, and a much larger observability ecosystem (Kibana, Beats, ingest pipelines) but ships under SSPL/Elastic License, which is why OpenSearch was forked. Practically: Solr suits schema-driven enterprise search with heavy faceting; Elasticsearch suits log/metric analytics and teams wanting the wider stack.
followUps: Why does Lucene make both near-real-time rather than real-time?
What is a shard vs a replica in SolrCloud?

questions.question: Documents are indexed into Solr but don't appear in search results for minutes. What do you check?
questions.answer: Lucene only exposes documents after a searcher reopens, so check the commit strategy: an update without commit is invisible, and a soft commit (openSearcher=true) is what makes documents visible while a hard commit flushes the transaction log to disk. If autoSoftCommit maxTime is set high (or missing) you get exactly this multi-minute lag; typical settings are autoSoftCommit around 1000ms and autoCommit around 15000ms with openSearcher=false. Also watch for commit-per-document from clients, which thrashes searcher warming and caches and makes latency worse, and check warmup queries and cache autowarmCount if the first queries after commit are slow.
followUps: Why is openSearcher=false used for the hard commit?
What does committing on every document do to the filter cache?

questions.question: Design real-time price updates for a trading UI showing 500 instruments, updating up to 50 times per second each.
questions.answer: Do not push every tick: 25k messages/s per client would saturate the browser. Conflate server-side by keeping the latest value per instrument and flushing a delta batch on a fixed tick (e.g. 10 Hz), sending only instruments the client has actually subscribed to and only fields that changed. Transport: WebSocket, because the client continuously changes its subscription set as it scrolls, and binary framing keeps payloads small. Fan-out comes from a broker topic per instrument group into the gateway layer, each gateway node holding the subscription map for its own sockets; on reconnect send a full snapshot plus a sequence number and then resume deltas, dropping any delta with a sequence gap and re-snapshotting.
followUps: How do you handle a slow consumer whose send buffer fills up?
Why is snapshot-plus-sequence better than replaying every delta?

questions.question: When is SSE a better choice than WebSocket for an LLM token stream or a notification feed?
questions.answer: When traffic is one-directional, SSE gives you automatic reconnect, Last-Event-ID resume and plain HTTP semantics for free — the same auth cookies, the same CDN, proxies and observability, and no separate upgrade path to secure. WebSocket would require you to hand-roll reconnect, resume and heartbeat logic and to make L7 proxies handle upgrades. SSE's real limits are that it is UTF-8 text only (binary needs base64), and that under HTTP/1.1 browsers cap ~6 connections per origin — HTTP/2 multiplexing removes that, so SSE is usually the right default for streaming responses and notifications.
followUps: What does SSE cost the server in held connections vs polling?
How would you send binary attachments alongside an SSE stream?

questions.question: How do you index data from your primary database into Solr or Elasticsearch without them drifting apart?
questions.answer: Treat the search index as a derived read model, never the source of truth. Push updates via CDC or a transactional outbox so an index write cannot be lost by a dual-write failure, key documents by primary key so indexing is idempotent, and include a monotonic version (updated_at or a sequence) using Solr's optimistic concurrency / Elasticsearch external versioning so an out-of-order update cannot overwrite a newer one. Run a periodic reconciliation job that compares counts and checksums per key range, and keep a documented full-reindex path (index to a new collection/alias, then swap the alias) because you will eventually change the schema or analyzers.
followUps: Why is alias swapping better than reindexing in place?
How do you detect drift before users report wrong results?

questions.question: What is the DOM, and how does it relate to the HTML a backend server sends?
questions.answer: The server sends HTML as text; the browser parses it into the DOM, an in-memory tree of nodes that JavaScript can read and mutate. The DOM is not the HTML source: the parser fixes malformed markup, and any JS mutation means the live DOM can diverge completely from what the server sent (which is why 'view source' and devtools Elements can differ). For a backend developer this matters for server-rendered templates, for HTML escaping (unescaped data becomes real DOM nodes, i.e. XSS), and for scrapers or tests that read raw HTML but miss JS-injected content.
followUps: Why does escaping depend on the context (HTML body, attribute, URL, JS)?
How would you test a page whose content only exists after JS runs?

questions.question: Explain how a browser-based frontend consumes a backend REST API, from fetch call to rendered data.
questions.answer: The frontend calls fetch('/api/orders', { headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ...' }, credentials: 'include' }), which returns a promise resolving to a Response; you check response.ok (fetch does not reject on 4xx/5xx) and then await response.json(). The backend contract that matters is a stable JSON shape, correct Content-Type, meaningful status codes, and pagination/filtering via query params. The UI then has to model three states explicitly - loading, error and empty - so backend error responses should be machine-readable (a stable code field, not just a prose message) and consistent across endpoints.
followUps: Why does fetch not throw on a 500?
How would you design an error body the frontend can localise?

questions.question: What are the essential CSS concepts a backend developer should know to work on server-rendered templates?
questions.answer: Selectors and specificity (inline > id > class > element, with !important overriding), the cascade and inheritance, and the box model (content, padding, border, margin, and box-sizing: border-box). Layout is dominated by flexbox for one-dimensional rows/columns and grid for two-dimensional layouts, with position: relative/absolute/fixed/sticky for out-of-flow elements and z-index/stacking contexts for overlap. Media queries handle responsiveness, and in templates the practical rules are: keep class names stable because tests and CSS both depend on them, and never build layout out of inline styles generated server-side.
followUps: What creates a new stacking context?
When do you reach for grid instead of flexbox?

questions.question: Explain the JavaScript event loop and why an API call does not block the UI.
questions.answer: JS runs single-threaded on a call stack; asynchronous work (network, timers) is handed to the host environment, and when it completes a callback is queued. The event loop drains the microtask queue (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) fully after each task, then takes the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, events), so a fetch never blocks rendering but a long synchronous loop does - it freezes the frame. This is the same model as Node.js, which is why a CPU-heavy handler in Node stalls every other request and belongs in a worker thread or a separate job.
followUps: Why does a promise chain run before a setTimeout(0)?
How do you keep a CPU-bound task from blocking a Node HTTP server?

questions.question: A frontend on https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com and the browser reports 'No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header'. Explain what is happening and fix it.
questions.answer: Those are different origins, so the browser applies CORS: the request is sent (or preflighted) but the response is hidden from JS unless the server returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin matching the origin. The fix is on the API, not the frontend: return Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com, plus Access-Control-Allow-Methods/Headers, and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true if cookies are used - and note that with credentials the wildcard * is illegal. Also make sure the error handler and any proxy/gateway emit these headers too, otherwise 4xx/5xx responses look like CORS failures and mask the real bug.
followUps: Why does CORS not protect the server itself?
What does Vary: Origin prevent when a CDN is in front?

questions.question: When does a browser send a CORS preflight, and what makes a request 'simple'?
questions.answer: A request is simple if the method is GET, HEAD or POST, the headers are limited to CORS-safelisted ones, and Content-Type is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain. Anything else - PUT, DELETE, PATCH, a custom header like X-Request-Id, or Content-Type: application/json - triggers an OPTIONS preflight carrying Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers, which the server must answer with matching Allow headers and ideally Access-Control-Max-Age so the result is cached (Chrome caps it at 2 hours). Preflights double latency on chatty APIs, so make sure the OPTIONS route is handled before auth middleware and never requires a token.
followUps: Why must the preflight response be unauthenticated?
How would you measure preflight overhead in production?

questions.question: Compare SSR, CSR, SSG and hydration, and what each implies for the backend.
questions.answer: CSR ships a near-empty HTML shell plus a JS bundle that fetches JSON and renders in the browser: light on the server, bad first paint and weak SEO without prerendering. SSR renders HTML per request on the server, giving fast first contentful paint and crawlable markup at the cost of server CPU, per-request data fetching latency and a cache story you must design. SSG prerenders at build time and serves from a CDN (with ISR/revalidation for freshness), ideal for content that changes rarely. Hydration attaches JS event handlers to server-rendered HTML; if the server and client render different output you get hydration mismatch errors, and the backend must ensure the data used for SSR and the data returned to the client API are consistent.
followUps: How does streaming SSR change TTFB?
Which auth model works for SSR - cookies or bearer tokens in memory?

questions.question: The frontend team says your API is 'slow' but your server-side p99 is 40ms. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: Server time is only one segment: reproduce in the browser Network panel and split the waterfall into DNS, TCP, TLS, waiting (TTFB) and content download, and check whether an OPTIONS preflight, a redirect chain (http -> https -> www) or a cold CDN is adding round trips. Then look at the call pattern: a chatty UI doing N sequential requests (a list plus one detail call per row) turns 40ms into seconds regardless of server speed, and a missing Cache-Control/ETag means every navigation refetches. Fix the real cause - collapse N+1 client calls into one endpoint or add batching/expansion params, cut redirects, enable compression and caching - and confirm with real-user monitoring, not local timings.
followUps: How do ETag and If-None-Match reduce payload without losing freshness?
When is it right to give the frontend a purpose-built aggregate endpoint (BFF)?

questions.question: Where should a SPA store an access token, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer: localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS exfiltrates the token; cookies with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite cannot be read by JS but are attached automatically, which reintroduces CSRF risk on state-changing requests. The common answer is a short-lived access token held in memory plus a refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict/Lax cookie scoped to the refresh endpoint, with rotation and reuse detection. Whichever you choose, the backend must still enforce CSRF protection for cookie auth (SameSite plus a double-submit or synchronizer token) and keep token lifetimes short enough that revocation is meaningful.
followUps: Why does CORS not stop CSRF?
How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?

questions.question: What is the difference between defer, async and a plain script tag, and why does it matter for page speed?
questions.answer: A plain <script src> blocks HTML parsing until it is fetched and executed, so it delays first paint. async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it arrives, interrupting parsing and running in unpredictable order - fine for independent third-party tags like analytics. defer downloads in parallel but executes in document order after parsing completes and before DOMContentLoaded, which is the right default for application code, as is type="module" (deferred by default). For a server-rendered page the practical rule is: critical CSS inline in <head>, app JS deferred at the end, third-party scripts async and ideally behind consent.
followUps: How do preload and preconnect hints fit in?
What does a render-blocking stylesheet cost on a slow 3G connection?

questions.question: A user reports that after deploying a new frontend build they still see the old broken UI, even after a refresh. What happened?
questions.answer: Stale caching of index.html or of a service worker: hashed asset bundles cache fine forever, but the HTML entry point must be served with Cache-Control: no-cache (or a very short max-age) so it is revalidated, otherwise the browser or CDN keeps pointing at deleted bundle hashes and you also see chunk-load errors. If a service worker is registered it can serve the whole shell from Cache Storage until it updates, so it needs a versioned cache name plus skipWaiting/clients.claim or an explicit update prompt. Fix: purge the CDN for the HTML, correct the cache headers per asset class, and keep old bundle files deployed for a grace period so in-flight sessions do not break mid-navigation.
followUps: Why keep old hashed chunks after a deploy?
How would you invalidate a service worker cache safely?

questions.question: Design the backend contract for a dashboard that must show live order status to thousands of concurrent users. Polling, SSE or WebSocket?
questions.answer: Short polling is simplest and cache-friendly but wastes requests and adds up to one interval of latency; Server-Sent Events give one-way server push over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume, and work through most proxies; WebSockets give full duplex but need their own upgrade path, auth handshake, heartbeats and sticky routing or a shared pub/sub backplane. For a read-only dashboard SSE is the right default: one HTTP/2 stream per user, events pushed from a Redis/Kafka fan-out, with an initial REST snapshot plus incremental events so a reconnect does not require replaying everything. Whatever the transport, the contract needs event ids for resumption, a heartbeat to survive idle proxy timeouts, and a documented backpressure/drop policy.
followUps: How do you authenticate and authorise an SSE or WebSocket connection?
What breaks when you run SSE behind HTTP/1.1 with a 6-connection-per-origin limit?

questions.question: Why is SHA-256 the wrong choice for storing passwords, and what should you use instead?
questions.answer: SHA-256 is designed to be fast - a GPU rig computes billions of hashes per second, so an offline attacker brute-forces common passwords from a leaked table almost instantly. Password hashing needs a deliberately slow, tunable function: bcrypt (Blowfish-based, cost factor, memory-light), scrypt (adds a memory-hard parameter N/r/p so GPUs and ASICs lose their advantage), or Argon2id (current OWASP recommendation, tunable memory, iterations and parallelism, resistant to both GPU and side-channel attacks). These also generate and embed a per-password salt automatically. Use SHA-256 for integrity and HMAC, never as a raw password store.
followUps: What Argon2id parameters does OWASP suggest as a baseline?
Why is HMAC-SHA256 fine for signing tokens but not for passwords?

questions.question: What do a salt, a pepper and a work factor each protect against?
questions.answer: A salt is a unique random value per password, stored alongside the hash; it defeats precomputed rainbow tables and ensures two users with the same password get different hashes, so cracking must be done one account at a time. A pepper is a secret value shared across all hashes but stored outside the database (in a KMS or app config); it means a database-only leak is not crackable at all, but it must be rotated carefully. The work factor (bcrypt cost, scrypt N, Argon2 memory/iterations) sets how expensive one guess is - target roughly 250-500ms per hash on your hardware and raise it as hardware improves.
followUps: Why must salts be random rather than the username?
How do you rotate a pepper without invalidating all passwords?

questions.question: Your legacy database has unsalted MD5 password hashes and bcrypt cost 8. How do you migrate without forcing every user to reset?
questions.answer: Wrap the old hash: store bcrypt(md5(password)) for existing rows, computable offline without users, and mark the row with an algorithm/version column. On next successful login you have the plaintext momentarily, so re-hash with Argon2id (or bcrypt at the new cost) and overwrite. Store the algorithm and parameters in the hash string itself so verification dispatches per row, and for the cost bump the same on-login rehash applies - bcrypt's `$2b$08$` prefix tells you the stored cost so you can compare it to the target. Note bcrypt truncates input at 72 bytes, so pre-hashing with a hex MD5 or SHA-256 digest is safe length-wise, but never pre-hash raw with base64 of SHA-512 without checking length. Force-reset only accounts you believe were breached.
followUps: Why does bcrypt's 72-byte limit matter for passphrases?
How do you avoid a timing side channel when the algorithm differs per user?

questions.question: Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake and what changed from TLS 1.2.
questions.answer: TLS 1.3 is one round trip: ClientHello carries the supported groups plus a key_share guess (usually X25519) and cipher suites; the server replies ServerHello with its key_share, and from there both sides derive the shared secret so EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished are already encrypted. TLS 1.2 needed two round trips and sent the certificate in the clear. TLS 1.3 also removes RSA key transport (forward secrecy is mandatory - ephemeral ECDHE only), drops CBC, RC4, compression and renegotiation, and cuts the cipher suite list to five AEAD suites. 0-RTT resumption sends application data in the first flight but is replayable, so restrict it to idempotent requests.
followUps: Why is 0-RTT data unsafe for a POST /transfer?
What does SNI reveal, and what does Encrypted Client Hello fix?

questions.question: Your service calls a partner API and suddenly gets 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority', but curl from your laptop works. How do you debug it?
questions.answer: The difference is the trust store, not the certificate. Reproduce with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -showcerts` and compare the chain your server receives against your laptop's: the common cause is the partner serving a leaf without the intermediate, which browsers and desktop curl paper over via AIA fetching or a cached intermediate, while a slim container image cannot. The second common cause is a container with no ca-certificates package installed, or an image built FROM scratch. Fixes: ask the partner to send the full chain, install ca-certificates in the image, and only pin or add a custom CA bundle deliberately - never set InsecureSkipVerify / verify=False, which disables authentication entirely and makes MITM trivial. Also check clock skew, since an expired-or-not-yet-valid error looks similar.
followUps: What is the difference between chain validation and hostname verification?
How would you detect an expiring certificate before it fires an incident?

questions.question: When is certificate pinning worth it, and what is the failure mode?
questions.answer: Pinning binds a client to a specific key or CA - typically pin the SPKI hash of the leaf or intermediate public key, not the certificate, so renewal with the same key does not break. It is worth it for mobile apps and service-to-service calls where you control both ends and want protection against a compromised or coerced CA, or against a user-installed MITM proxy. The failure mode is a self-inflicted outage: if the pinned key is rotated or revoked and clients cannot be updated (app store review takes days), every client hard-fails. Mitigate with at least one backup pin for a key you hold offline, a short pin lifetime, and a remote kill switch. HPKP, the HTTP header version, was removed from browsers precisely because of this bricking risk; use certificate transparency monitoring plus CAA records instead for the web.
followUps: Why pin the SPKI rather than the whole certificate?
How does Certificate Transparency detect mis-issuance?

questions.question: What does HSTS do that a 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS does not?
questions.answer: A redirect still allows one plaintext request, which an on-path attacker can intercept and strip (sslstrip), serving the user a plain HTTP version forever. `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` tells the browser to rewrite every future request to that host to HTTPS internally, before it hits the network, and to refuse click-through on certificate errors. The gap is the very first visit, which preload solves: adding the `preload` directive and submitting to hstspreload.org ships the domain in the browser binary. Cost: once preloaded you cannot serve any subdomain over plain HTTP, and removal takes months, so roll out with a short max-age first.
followUps: Why is includeSubDomains risky with internal-only subdomains?
What other security headers would you set alongside HSTS?

questions.question: Explain injection with a concrete SQL and a concrete command example, and the correct fix for each.
questions.answer: SQL: `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='" + input + "'"` with input `' OR '1'='1' --` dumps the table. The fix is parameterized queries / prepared statements, where the driver sends the SQL and the values separately so the value can never become syntax; escaping by hand and blocklists both fail on encodings and quirks. Identifiers (table and column names) cannot be parameterized, so validate them against an allowlist. Command injection: `os.system("convert " + filename)` with filename `a.png; rm -rf /` - fix by using the exec-array form (`subprocess.run(["convert", filename], shell=False)`) so no shell parses the string. The same principle covers NoSQL (reject operator objects like {"$ne": null} from JSON input), LDAP and template injection: never concatenate untrusted data into an interpreter's grammar.
followUps: Why does an ORM not automatically make you safe?
How would you detect existing injection points in a large codebase?

questions.question: A pentest finds that any authenticated user can fetch GET /api/invoices/{id} for any id. What class of bug is this and how do you fix it properly?
questions.answer: Broken access control - specifically IDOR / BOLA, the number one item in the OWASP Top 10 and OWASP API Top 10. Authentication passed; authorization was never checked against the object owner. The wrong fixes are switching to UUIDs (security through obscurity - ids leak via logs, referers and other endpoints) or hiding the link in the UI. The right fix is a server-side ownership check on every object access, ideally enforced structurally: scope the query itself (`WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?`) or use a centralized policy layer (Casbin, OPA, Rails Pundit) that every handler must call, deny by default. Then add a regression test per endpoint that a user from tenant B gets 404 (not 403, which confirms existence) and audit every other endpoint taking an id.
followUps: Why return 404 rather than 403 for another tenant's resource?
How do you catch IDOR automatically in CI?

questions.question: Your service fetches a user-supplied image URL to generate thumbnails. Explain the SSRF risk and a defense that actually holds.
questions.answer: An attacker submits `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` and your server, which sits inside the VPC with an instance role, returns cloud credentials - or hits internal admin endpoints, `http://localhost:9200`, or `file:///etc/passwd`. Blocklisting strings fails: DNS rebinding, decimal/octal IP encodings, `[::1]`, redirects to 127.0.0.1, and `0.0.0.0` all bypass it. A defense that holds: allowlist schemes (http/https only) and hosts, resolve the DNS name yourself, reject any resolved address in private/loopback/link-local ranges, then connect to that exact validated IP with the Host header set (pinning resolution to defeat rebinding), disable redirects or re-validate each hop, and cap size and timeout. Layer on network isolation - run the fetcher in an egress-restricted subnet behind a proxy and require IMDSv2, which requires a PUT-obtained token that SSRF cannot send.
followUps: Why does IMDSv2's hop limit of 1 also block containerized SSRF?
How does DNS rebinding beat a validate-then-fetch implementation?

questions.question: Explain how CORS actually works, including when a preflight is sent.
questions.answer: CORS is a browser mechanism that relaxes the same-origin policy for JavaScript reading cross-origin responses. Simple requests (GET/HEAD/POST with only CORS-safelisted headers and a content type of form-urlencoded, multipart or text/plain) are sent directly, and the browser hides the response unless `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matches. Anything else - PUT/DELETE/PATCH, `Content-Type: application/json`, a custom header like Authorization or X-Request-Id - triggers a preflight `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`; the server must answer with matching `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`/`-Headers` and may cache it via `Access-Control-Max-Age`. For cookies you need `credentials: 'include'` plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and a specific origin - the wildcard `*` is illegal with credentials. `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` is needed before JS can read non-safelisted response headers.
followUps: Why must you add `Vary: Origin` when reflecting the origin?
Why do curl and mobile apps ignore CORS entirely?

questions.question: A developer sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on an internal API and says CORS now secures it. Why is that wrong, and what is the real danger?
questions.answer: CORS is not authorization - it only tells a browser whether page JavaScript may read a response. It does not stop the request from being sent and processed (a non-preflighted POST still executes server-side), and it is irrelevant to curl, Postman, server-to-server calls and mobile apps, which never enforce it. Authorization must be a server-side check of the caller's identity and permissions on every request. The real danger in the other direction is a permissive config: reflecting any `Origin` header while also sending `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` lets any malicious site read authenticated responses on behalf of a logged-in victim - a full account data leak. Use a strict allowlist of origins, add `Vary: Origin`, and never reflect `null`.
followUps: How does a permissive CORS policy interact with CSRF defenses?
Which requests bypass preflight and therefore still hit your handler?

questions.question: Design a Content-Security-Policy for an app that currently uses inline scripts and a few CDNs.
questions.answer: Target `default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-{random}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'`. Generate a cryptographically random nonce per response, put it on every legitimate `<script nonce=...>` tag, and never on user-controllable markup - a per-response nonce means injected script has no valid nonce and is blocked. `'strict-dynamic'` lets a trusted script load its own dependencies, which removes the need to maintain a CDN host allowlist (host allowlists are commonly bypassable via JSONP endpoints or hosted user content). `frame-ancestors` replaces X-Frame-Options. Roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` plus `report-to` first, fix the violations, refactor inline event handlers (`onclick=`) into addEventListener since a nonce cannot cover them, then enforce. CSP is defense in depth - contextual output encoding remains the primary XSS fix.
followUps: Why is a hash-based CSP awkward for dynamically rendered scripts?
What does 'unsafe-inline' do to a nonce-based policy in older browsers?

questions.question: How would you harden a production Linux server and manage its secrets?
questions.answer: Least privilege first: the app runs as a dedicated non-root user with no shell, on a read-only filesystem where possible, with Linux capabilities dropped (`CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` only if it must bind port 80) and systemd hardening (`NoNewPrivileges`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `PrivateTmp`). Network: default-deny inbound in the security group and firewall, SSH by key only with `PasswordAuthentication no` and `PermitRootLogin no`, reachable only via a bastion or SSM Session Manager, plus automatic security updates and a minimal base image. Secrets never live in the repo, in environment variables baked into an image, or in a Dockerfile layer - store them in Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or SOPS-encrypted files, inject at runtime, scope each credential to one workload with short-lived dynamic credentials or a workload identity (IRSA, instance role), and rotate automatically. Add secret scanning (gitleaks) in CI, audit logging of every secret access, and a documented rotation runbook for when one leaks.
followUps: Why are env-var secrets readable from /proc and crash dumps?
How do short-lived dynamic database credentials change the blast radius of a leak?

questions.question: Where does an AI coding assistant reliably help a backend developer, and where does it not?
questions.answer: It helps most where the answer is well-specified and verifiable: boilerplate and glue, test scaffolding, migrations from a schema, parsing/serialization code, unfamiliar API usage, regexes and SQL you can immediately run, code explanations, and first-draft docs. It is weakest where correctness depends on context the model cannot see or verify: concurrency and locking, security-sensitive logic, performance work that needs measurement, cross-service contracts, and anything depending on internal conventions or production behavior. Practical rule: use it where a test or a run can prove the output, and be sceptical where the failure mode is silent.
followUps: Which categories of bug does generated code most often introduce?
How would you measure whether it actually speeds your team up?

questions.question: What is a hallucinated API, and how do you catch it before it reaches review?
questions.answer: The model emits a plausible but nonexistent function, parameter, config key, or library — for example a method that existed in an older major version, or a flag invented to fit the request. Catch it mechanically rather than by reading: compile or type-check, run the code, and let the linter flag unresolved symbols; verify the identifier against the installed version's documentation or source (not memory), and confirm the package itself exists and is the one you mean. Hallucinated package names are also a supply-chain risk — attackers publish them (slopsquatting), so never install a dependency just because generated code imported it.
followUps: Why is a passing type-check not sufficient for a semantic hallucination?
What is slopsquatting and how do you defend against it?

questions.question: How do you review AI-generated code differently from human-written code?
questions.answer: Assume confident-looking but unverified code. Check first that the problem being solved is the right one, since the model optimizes for a plausible answer to the prompt, not the requirement. Then look for the characteristic failure patterns: missing error handling and edge cases, ignored cancellation/timeouts, silent swallowing of exceptions, off-by-one and empty-collection cases, missing input validation, subtly wrong SQL (N+1, unindexed predicate, missing transaction), invented APIs, duplicated logic that already exists in the codebase, and tests that assert the implementation rather than the behavior. Run it, read the diff line by line, and never merge code you could not have written and cannot explain.
followUps: Why is 'tests pass' weak evidence when the tests were also generated?
Who is accountable for a bug in generated code?

questions.question: What are the legal and confidentiality risks of AI-assisted coding, and how do you manage them?
questions.answer: Two distinct risks. Outbound: source code, credentials, customer data, or personal data leaving your boundary in prompts — manage with an approved vendor and data-processing terms, zero-retention or no-training settings, secret scanning before sending, exclusion rules for sensitive paths (.env, key material), and a policy people actually know. Inbound: generated code may reproduce licensed code, creating copyleft or attribution obligations, and provenance is unclear. Manage with license scanning of the codebase, a policy that generated code is treated as your own contribution and reviewed and tested as such, and awareness of the vendor's indemnity terms. Both belong in a written internal policy, not in individual judgement.
followUps: Which repository paths would you exclude from assistant context?
How would you detect license-incompatible code entering the repo?

questions.question: What does 'context management' mean when working with a coding assistant, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The model can only reason over what is in its context window, so results are dominated by what you put there and what you leave out. Practically: give the actual interface definitions, schema, and error messages rather than describing them; include the one or two files that set conventions; state constraints (language version, library, style, performance budget) explicitly; and remove irrelevant files, because noise degrades output and costs tokens. Long sessions drift — restate the goal, or start a fresh session for a new task. Repo-level instruction files (conventions, architecture, commands) are how you make this repeatable rather than per-prompt effort.
followUps: What belongs in a repo-level instructions file?
Why can adding more files make output worse?

questions.question: An assistant produces a 900-line refactor across 15 files that compiles and passes tests. Do you merge it?
questions.answer: Not as one PR. You cannot review 900 lines across 15 files effectively, and 'tests pass' only proves the existing tests still hold — which is precisely the weak evidence if the refactor changed behavior the tests do not cover. Ask for it in reviewable slices: mechanical moves and renames separately from behavioral change, one module at a time, each independently deployable. Verify coverage over the touched paths before trusting green CI, run the service and exercise the real flows, and check that the refactor did not quietly change error handling, transaction boundaries, or public contracts. If it cannot be split, that is a signal the change is too coupled to land at once.
followUps: How would you verify behavior preservation beyond the existing tests?
What would make you accept a large generated change?

questions.question: When should you not use an AI assistant on a task?
questions.answer: When you cannot verify the result, when the cost of a subtle error is high and detection is slow, or when learning is the point. Concretely: security-critical logic (auth, crypto, access control) without expert review; incident response where you need certainty about the running system rather than plausible narrative; anything requiring data you must not send to a third party; performance work that must be driven by measurements; and decisions about architecture or domain rules that require organizational context. Also avoid it as a substitute for reading the documentation of a system you will own for years.
followUps: How can it still help safely during an incident?
Where does it hurt a junior developer's growth?

questions.question: Your team's velocity looks flat after adopting an assistant, while everyone reports feeling faster. How do you evaluate it honestly?
questions.answer: Separate perception from outcome and measure the whole pipeline, not typing speed. Track delivery metrics over a period long enough to be meaningful: lead time from first commit to production, deployment frequency, change failure rate, and mean time to restore, plus review throughput and PR size. Faster generation often shifts the bottleneck to review and testing, or trades throughput for more rework and post-release defects, so watch revert rate, hotfix count, and bug escape rate. Run it as a comparison (before/after or team-vs-team) with confounders named, and ask where people stopped verifying. Being 'faster' while change failure rate rises is not an improvement.
followUps: Which metric would first reveal quality erosion?
How do you avoid Goodharting these metrics?

questions.question: What guardrails let an agentic assistant run commands in a repository safely?
questions.answer: Constrain blast radius rather than trusting intent. Run it in an isolated workspace — a container, VM, or git worktree — with no production credentials and no write access to shared infrastructure; use read-only or dev-only database copies. Require explicit approval for irreversible or outward-facing actions: force-push, dependency installs, migrations, deploys, network calls, deleting files. Keep changes on a branch behind normal PR review and CI; never let the agent bypass branch protection or push to main. Log every command it ran so the diff is auditable, and cap cost and runtime so a loop cannot run unbounded.
followUps: Which actions would you always gate behind human approval?
Why is a separate worktree or container worth the setup?

questions.question: How do you use an assistant to write tests without ending up with worthless tests?
questions.answer: Give it the behavior contract, not the implementation, or it will assert what the code already does — including the bug. Write or specify the cases yourself (happy path, boundary, empty, error, concurrency) and let it fill in mechanics and fixtures. Verify the tests actually discriminate: make them fail deliberately by mutating the implementation, or use mutation testing; a test that passes against a broken implementation is noise. Reject over-mocked tests that assert call sequences rather than outcomes, and keep test naming and structure to your existing conventions so the suite stays readable.
followUps: Why does generating tests from implementation lock in bugs?
How does mutation testing validate a generated suite?

questions.question: What does a genuinely useful code review comment look like?
questions.answer: It states the problem, the consequence, and a concrete alternative, and it is about the code, not the author: 'this query runs inside the loop, so a 100-item request becomes 100 round trips — fetch the ids once and batch with WHERE id IN (...)'. Distinguish severity explicitly: blocking correctness or security issues, versus 'nit:' style preferences, versus 'question:' where you are asking, not asserting. Praise what is genuinely good so the signal is not only negative, and prefer a suggestion the author can apply over an abstract principle. If a thread exceeds two round trips, move it to a call.
followUps: How do you label nits so they do not block a merge?
What do you do when a review thread stalls in disagreement?

questions.question: What do you actually look for when reviewing a backend pull request, in priority order?
questions.answer: First, is this the right change for the requirement, and does the design fit the existing architecture — a correct implementation of the wrong thing is the expensive mistake. Then correctness and edge cases; security (authorization on the new endpoint, input validation, injection, data exposure in responses and logs); data layer concerns (transaction boundaries, index for the new predicate, N+1, migration safety and backward compatibility during rollout); failure behavior (timeouts, retries, idempotency); observability (does a failure here produce a usable log or metric); test quality; and only last naming, structure, and style — most of which a formatter and linter should enforce so humans do not spend review capacity on it.
followUps: Which of these can be automated away entirely?
How does review focus change for a migration-only PR?

questions.question: Reviews in your team take three days and PRs are averaging 1,200 lines. How do you fix the pipeline?
questions.answer: Attack size and latency together, because large PRs cause slow reviews and slow reviews cause authors to batch more work. Set a soft size limit and teach splitting (interface first, then implementation, then callers; mechanical changes separate; feature flags to land incomplete work safely). Make review an explicit expectation with a target response time (e.g. first response within four hours) rather than leftover time, and use round-robin or load-based reviewer assignment so it does not all land on one senior. Move style and obvious defects to automation — formatter, linter, static analysis, required checks — and reserve human review for design, correctness, and security. Measure PR size, time-to-first-review, and time-to-merge to confirm the change worked.
followUps: How do feature flags enable smaller PRs?
Which metric tells you reviewers are overloaded?

questions.question: How do you review a database migration differently from application code?
questions.answer: Migrations are the changes that cannot simply be rolled back with a redeploy, so review for deployment order and reversibility. Check it is expand-contract: add nullable columns or new tables first, deploy code that writes both, backfill in batches, switch reads, and only drop the old column in a later release. Check locking behavior on the target engine — adding a NOT NULL column with a default, changing a type, or creating an index without CONCURRENTLY can lock a large table and take the service down. Check the backfill is batched with bounded transactions and is restartable, that the down migration exists and is safe, and that the new query predicate has a supporting index.
followUps: Why must the code tolerate both schema versions?
Which migration operations would you never run in one transaction?

questions.question: Which documentation should be generated from code, and which must be written by hand?
questions.answer: Generate what is mechanically derivable and goes stale instantly otherwise: API reference from the OpenAPI/protobuf/GraphQL schema, client SDKs from that same schema, type and docstring references, database schema diagrams, configuration and environment-variable tables, changelogs from conventional commits, and architecture dependency graphs. Write by hand what encodes intent and cannot be derived: why the system is shaped this way (ADRs), onboarding and getting-started guides, runbooks, domain glossaries, and worked examples of common tasks. Generated docs answer 'what are the fields'; handwritten docs answer 'what should I do and why'.
followUps: How do you keep generated docs from drifting from the deployed version?
What makes a good ADR?

questions.question: Your API docs are perpetually out of date. How do you fix that structurally?
questions.answer: Make the schema the single source of truth and enforce it in CI. Either spec-first (the OpenAPI document is reviewed, the server validates requests against it, and handlers are generated or checked from it) or code-first with annotations that generate the spec — but in both cases a CI job regenerates the spec and fails the build if the committed artifact differs, so drift cannot merge. Publish docs automatically on deploy from the deployed commit, run contract tests and example requests against a live instance so wrong examples break the build, and add a lint step (Spectral) for descriptions, error shapes, and naming. Documentation that is not verified by a pipeline will always drift.
followUps: What are the trade-offs of spec-first versus code-first?
How do contract tests keep examples honest?

questions.question: What is the definition of refactoring, and what makes a refactor safe?
questions.answer: Refactoring changes the internal structure of code without changing its observable behavior. Safety comes from three things: characterization tests that pin current behavior before you touch anything (including the odd behavior you might not intend to keep), small reversible steps that keep the system green after each one, and automated tooling (IDE rename, extract method) over hand-editing. Never mix refactoring with behavior change in the same commit — when something breaks you must be able to tell which one caused it. Where tests are missing, add them first at the boundary you are about to change, or use a parallel-run/comparison harness against the old path.
followUps: What is a characterization test?
Why separate refactoring commits from feature commits?

questions.question: You must refactor a 3,000-line service class with no tests, in production, handling money. How do you proceed?
questions.answer: Do not start by editing it. First establish a safety net: add characterization tests at the class boundary capturing current outputs for real recorded inputs, including the edge cases found in the data; add logging or metrics around the paths you will change. Then carve out behavior incrementally with the sprout/wrap technique — new logic in new tested units called from the old class, or a facade in front of it — rather than a rewrite. Use the strangler-fig approach for larger seams, and for money paths run the new implementation in shadow mode alongside the old, comparing results without acting on them, until discrepancies are zero. Ship small, keep every step deployable and revertible behind a flag, and never refactor and change pricing logic in the same release.
followUps: What is shadow/parallel running and what does it cost?
When is a rewrite actually the right call?

questions.question: How do you justify refactoring work to a product owner who wants features?
questions.answer: Frame it in delivery terms, not aesthetics: name the specific cost the current structure imposes — lead time on changes in this module, the recurring class of production incidents it causes, onboarding time, or the features that are effectively blocked. Bring evidence: incident and hotfix counts by area, cycle time for changes touching that code, and the concrete upcoming roadmap item it obstructs. Propose it scoped and incremental — a bounded piece attached to the feature that needs it, with a defined outcome and a stopping point — rather than an open-ended 'cleanup quarter', which is where trust in refactoring gets destroyed. Agree a small standing allocation so it does not require re-negotiation every time.
followUps: Which evidence is most persuasive in practice?
Why do big-bang cleanup projects usually fail politically?

questions.question: Which code smells most reliably signal a needed refactor in backend code?
questions.answer: The ones tied to change cost: a class or module that every feature must touch (shotgun surgery / god object), duplicated business rules that drift out of sync, long parameter lists and boolean flags controlling behavior, deeply nested conditionals encoding domain rules that belong in the domain layer, primitive obsession where money or ids are raw strings and floats, feature envy where a service reaches into another object's data, and business logic leaking into controllers or ORM models. A practical prioritizer is churn multiplied by complexity — refactor the files that are both complicated and changed constantly, and ignore the ugly module nobody has edited in two years.
followUps: Why is churn x complexity a better signal than complexity alone?
Why is money-as-float a correctness bug, not a style issue?

questions.question: Why stream a model response to the client instead of returning it in one response?
questions.answer: Generation takes seconds to minutes, so a single response means the user stares at a spinner and you hold a request open long enough to hit proxy and load-balancer timeouts. Streaming tokens as they are produced cuts time-to-first-byte to a few hundred milliseconds, makes the wait tolerable, and lets the user cancel early — which also saves output tokens and money. It also avoids buffering a large payload in memory. The cost is complexity: partial output must be handled, errors can occur mid-stream after a 200 status, and every hop (nginx, CDN, API gateway) must not buffer the body.
followUps: How do you report an error that happens after streaming has started?
Which nginx settings break streaming?

questions.question: Design token streaming from your backend to a browser over SSE. What are the mechanics?
followUps: Why is SSE often preferred to WebSocket here?
How do you stop generation when the client disappears?

questions.question: Your streaming endpoint works locally but clients receive the whole response at once in production. Diagnose it.
questions.answer: Something between the application and the browser is buffering. Check in order: nginx `proxy_buffering on` (disable for that location or set `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), gzip/compression middleware that buffers to compress, an API gateway or CDN that does not support streaming responses, and application-level response buffering or a framework wrapper that collects the body. Also verify your handler actually flushes per chunk rather than relying on the writer's internal buffer, and that no middleware (logging, error wrapper) reads the body. Confirm the hop-by-hop behavior with `curl -N` directly against each layer to find where chunking stops.
followUps: Why does gzip interact badly with streaming?
How do you test each hop in isolation?

questions.question: What are structured outputs, and how do they differ from asking a model for JSON in the prompt?
questions.answer: Structured outputs constrain generation to a supplied JSON Schema (constrained decoding / grammar-based sampling) so the result is guaranteed parseable and schema-conformant; prompting for JSON only makes it likely, and you will eventually get prose preamble, markdown fences, trailing commas, or a truncated object. Structured outputs remove the parsing class of failure entirely, but not semantic error — the model can still return a well-typed wrong value, a hallucinated enum member that you must therefore express as an enum, or plausible nulls. Design the schema tightly (enums instead of free strings, required fields, no additional properties) and still validate business invariants after parsing.
followUps: Which validation must still happen after a schema-valid parse?
How does a tight enum reduce hallucination?

questions.question: How do you build a reliable extraction endpoint where the model must return a schema-conformant object?
questions.answer: Validate every response against the schema at the boundary (Pydantic, zod, JSON Schema) and treat validation failure as a retryable error: retry with the validation error fed back as context, with a small bounded number of attempts, exponential backoff and jitter, and a dead-letter path that stores the raw output for inspection rather than silently returning a default. Keep the schema and prompt versioned together so you can attribute quality changes, log input, raw output, and validation result for offline evaluation, and set a max-tokens ceiling high enough that truncation is not the cause of malformed output. For anything consequential, add business-rule checks and a confidence or 'unknown' branch rather than forcing the model to guess.
followUps: Why cap retries rather than loop until valid?
How does an explicit 'unknown' option improve accuracy?

questions.question: What is function/tool calling, and who executes the function?
questions.answer: You describe available functions to the model as a name, description, and JSON Schema of parameters; the model returns a structured request to call one with arguments instead of prose. Your backend executes it — the model has no access to anything — then returns the result, and the model continues with that context, possibly calling more tools. Consequences: the model's output is untrusted input to your code, so arguments must be validated and authorized exactly like an external API request; execution must be idempotent or guarded because the loop may retry; and each turn costs tokens, so tool count and result size directly drive latency and cost.
followUps: Why treat tool arguments as untrusted input?
What limits how many tools you should expose at once?

questions.question: How do you design a good tool interface for a model?
questions.answer: Design it like an API for a capable but context-poor consumer. Few, coarse-grained, task-shaped tools beat many fine-grained ones (`search_orders(customer_id, status, date_range)` rather than five overlapping getters), because selection accuracy falls as the tool list grows. Names and descriptions must state when to use it and when not to, parameters should be enums and typed values rather than free strings, and required fields must be genuinely required. Return compact, structured results with only the fields needed — full database rows blow up the context — and return actionable error messages the model can recover from ('customer_id not found, call search_customers first') rather than a stack trace. Make reads cheap and writes explicitly confirmable.
followUps: Why do too many tools degrade selection accuracy?
How should a tool report a recoverable error?

questions.question: A tool-calling agent loops, calling the same tool 40 times, and your bill spikes. What controls do you add?
questions.answer: Bound the loop structurally rather than hoping for better prompting: a maximum number of tool-call iterations per request, a total token and wall-clock budget enforced by the orchestration layer, and detection of repeated identical calls (hash the tool name plus arguments) that breaks the loop and returns a clear failure. Add per-tool timeouts and per-user rate limits and cost quotas, cache identical read-only tool results within a request, and log the full call trace so you can see where reasoning went in circles. Alert on cost per request and on the iteration-count distribution, not just on the monthly total — by the time the invoice shows it, the incident is a week old.
followUps: What is the right behavior when the iteration cap is hit?
Which signal detects this in minutes rather than days?

questions.question: How do you handle timeouts, retries, and idempotency when calling a slow external model API?
questions.answer: Set an explicit timeout well above p99 generation time but bounded, and derive it from a request-level deadline propagated through the call chain so a slow upstream cannot exceed the client's own budget. Retry only on transient conditions — 429, 5xx, connection errors — with exponential backoff plus jitter and a small attempt cap, honoring Retry-After; never blind-retry a timeout on a non-idempotent operation. Attach an idempotency key so a retried request that actually succeeded upstream does not double-charge or double-write, and record the request state before calling. Protect the rest of the system with a circuit breaker, a bulkhead (separate connection pool and concurrency limit), and a degraded fallback such as a cached or non-model response.
followUps: Why is retrying a timeout riskier than retrying a 503?
What does the bulkhead protect here?

questions.question: A user request needs a 90-second model job. How do you expose that through your HTTP API?
questions.answer: Do not hold a synchronous request open for 90 seconds — proxies, load balancers, and mobile networks will cut it, and retries will duplicate the work. Use the asynchronous job pattern: POST creates the job, returns `202 Accepted` with a job id and a status URL (Location header), and the work runs on a queue with a worker; the client polls `GET /jobs/{id}` or subscribes via SSE/WebSocket for completion, or you call a webhook with a signed payload. Accept an idempotency key on the POST so a retried submit returns the existing job instead of starting a second one, persist job state with timestamps and failure reason, expose progress if available, and support cancellation so abandoned work stops burning tokens.
followUps: When would you choose a webhook over polling?
How do you make job submission idempotent?

questions.question: What is prompt injection, and what does it mean for a backend exposing tools to a model?
questions.answer: Untrusted content that the model reads — a user message, a fetched web page, a support ticket, a document, a database field — contains instructions that redirect the model's behavior, for example telling it to call the delete tool or to include another tenant's data in its answer. Because the model cannot reliably distinguish data from instructions, the defense must be outside the model: authorize every tool call against the end user's own permissions rather than a service-wide credential, keep high-impact actions behind explicit human confirmation, allowlist outbound network destinations to prevent exfiltration, validate and constrain tool arguments, and never let model output become a privileged command or raw SQL. Treat all model output as untrusted input to the next system.
followUps: Why is prompt-level 'ignore malicious instructions' not a control?
How does per-user authorization on tools limit the damage?
